title.la: De Gradibus Humilitatis et Superbiae Tractatus
title.en: The Treatise on the Steps of Humility and Pride

title.la: Pars prima: de via humilitatis ad veritatem
title.en: Part I: The way of humility to truth

title.la: Praefatio
title.en: Preface

segments.la: Rogasti me, frater Godefride, ut ea quae de gradibus humilitatis coram fratribus locutus fueram, pleniori tibi tractatu dissererem. Cui tuae petitioni digne, ut dignum erat, et volens satisfacere, et timens non posse, evangelici consilii memor, non prius, fateor, incipere ausus sum, quam sedens computavi, si sufficerent sumptus ad perficiendum (Luc. xiv, 28).
segments.en: You asked me, brother Godfrey, to set out more fully, in a treatise for you, those things I had spoken before the brethren concerning the steps of humility. I wished to answer your request as it deserved, and I feared I could not. Mindful of the evangelist’s counsel, I confess I did not dare to begin until I had sat down and reckoned whether I had the means to finish (Luke 14:28).

segments.la: Cum autem charitas hunc foras misisset timorem, quo mihi timebam illudi de opere non consummando, subintravit alius timor de contrario, quo coepi timere gravius periculum de gloria si perfecissem, quam de ignominia si defecissem. Unde inter hunc timorem et charitatem, velut in quodam bivio positus, diu haesitavi, cui viarum tuto me crederem; metuens aut loquendo utiliter de humilitate, ipse humilis non inveniri; aut tacendo humiliter, inutilis fieri.
segments.en: When charity had cast out that fear of being mocked for an unfinished work, another fear came in from the opposite side: I began to dread a heavier danger from glory if I finished than from disgrace if I failed. So between this fear and charity, as at a fork in the road, I hesitated long which way I might safely trust—afraid that by speaking usefully of humility I might myself be found not humble, or that by keeping a humble silence I might become useless.

segments.la: Cumque neutram viam tutam, alterutram tamen mihi tenendam esse conspicerem, elegi potius tibi, si quem possem, communicare fructum sermonis, quam tutari me solum portu silentii: simul fiduciam habens, si quid forte quod approbes, dixerim, tuis precibus posse me non superbire; sin autem (quod magis puto) nihil tuo studio dignum effecerim, de nihilo superbire non posse.
segments.en: And seeing that neither way was safe, yet that I must take one of them, I chose rather to share with you, if I could, the fruit of the discourse, than to keep myself alone in the harbor of silence—trusting that if I happen to say something you approve, your prayers may keep me from pride; but if (as I rather think) I produce nothing worthy of your zeal, I cannot be proud of nothing.

title.la: Christum esse viam humilitatis, quo pervenitur ad veritatem
title.en: That Christ is the way of humility by which one comes to truth

segments.la: Locuturus ergo de gradibus humilitatis, quos beatus Benedictus non numerandos, sed ascendendos proponit (Reg. cap. 7), prius ostendo, si possum, quo per illos perveniendum sit, ut audito fructu perventionis, minus gravet labor ascensionis.
segments.en: I am about to speak of the steps of humility, which blessed Benedict sets before us not to be counted but to be climbed (Rule, ch. 7). First I show, if I can, where those steps lead, so that once the fruit of arrival is heard, the labor of ascent may weigh less.

segments.la: Proponat itaque Dominus nobis viae laborem, laboris mercedem. Ego sum, inquit, via, veritas, et vita (Ioan. xiv, 6). Viam dicit humilitatem, quae ducit ad veritatem. Altera labor, altera fructus laboris est.
segments.en: Let the Lord then set before us the labor of the way and the reward of the labor. I am, he says, the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6). By “way” he means humility, which leads to truth. The one is labor; the other is the fruit of labor.

segments.la: Unde sciam, inquis, quod ibi de humilitate locutus sit, cum indeterminate dixerit: Ego sum via? Audi apertius: Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde (Matth. xi, 29). Se ergo proponit humilitatis exemplum, mansuetudinis formam. Si imitaris eum, non ambulas in tenebris, sed habebis lumen vitae (Ioan. viii, 12).
segments.en: “How am I to know,” you ask, “that he was speaking of humility there, when he said indefinitely, I am the way?” Hear him more openly: Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart (Matt. 11:29). He therefore offers himself as the pattern of humility, the form of meekness. If you imitate him, you do not walk in darkness, but you will have the light of life (John 8:12).

segments.la: Quid est lumen vitae, nisi veritas, quae illuminans omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, ostendit ubi sit vera vita? Ideo cum dixisset, Ego sum via et veritas, subdidit, et vita: ac si diceret: Ego sum via, quae ad veritatem duco; ego sum veritas quae vitam promitto; ego sum vita, quam do.
segments.en: What is the light of life, if not truth, which, lighting every man who comes into this world, shows where true life is? Therefore when he had said, I am the way and the truth, he added, and the life—as if to say: I am the way who lead to truth; I am the truth who promise life; I am the life which I give.

segments.la: Haec est enim, ait, vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum, et quem misisti Iesum Christum (Matth. xviii, 3 / Ioan. xvii, 3).
segments.en: For this, he says, is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

segments.la: Viam considero, id est humilitatem: fructum desidero, veritatem. Sed quid si tantus est labor viae, ut ad optatum lucrum non possim pervenire? Respondet: Ego sum vita, id est viaticum, quo sustentaris in via. Clamat igitur errantibus, et viam ignorantibus, Ego sum via: dubitantibus, et non credentibus, Ego sum veritas: iam ascendentibus, sed lassescentibus, Ego sum vita. Satis, ut reor, ostensum est ex proposito capitulo Evangelii, cognitionem veritatis fructum esse humilitatis. Accipe et aliud. Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine caeli et terrae, quia abscondisti haec, haud dubium quin veritatis secreta, a sapientibus et prudentibus, id est a superbis, et revelasti ea parvulis (Luc. x, 21): hoc est humilibus. Et in hoc apparet quod veritas, quae superbis absconditur, humilibus revelatur.
segments.en: I consider the way, that is humility; I desire the fruit, truth. But what if the labor of the way is so great that I cannot reach the hoped-for gain? He answers: I am the life, that is, the provision by which you are sustained on the way. So he cries to those who wander and do not know the road, I am the way; to those who doubt and do not believe, I am the truth; to those already climbing but growing weary, I am the life. Enough, I think, has been shown from this Gospel chapter: knowledge of the truth is the fruit of humility. Take another word also. I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things—no doubt the secrets of truth—from the wise and prudent, that is from the proud, and have revealed them to little ones (Luke 10:21): that is, to the humble. And in this it appears that the truth which is hidden from the proud is revealed to the humble.

segments.la: Humilitatis vero talis potest esse definitio: Humilitas est virtus, qua homo verissima sui agnitione sibi ipsi vilescit. Haec autem convenit his qui ascensionibus in corde suo dispositis, de virtute in virtutem, id est de gradu in gradum proficiunt, donec ad culmen humilitatis perveniant, in quo velut in Sion, id est in speculatione, positi, veritatem prospiciant. Etenim, inquit, benedictionem dabit legislator (Psal. lxxxiii, 8): quia qui dedit legem, dabit et benedictionem; hoc est, qui iussit humilitatem, perdocet ad veritatem. Quis vero est hic legislator, nisi dulcis et rectus Dominus qui legem dedit delinquentibus in via? (Psal. xxiv, 8.) In via quippe delinquunt, qui veritatem derelinquunt. Sed numquid vel sic a dulci Domino derelinquuntur? Ipsis ergo dulcis et rectus Dominus legem dat viam humilitatis, per quam redeant ad cognitionem veritatis. Dat occasionem recuperandae salutis, quia dulcis est; non tamen absque disciplina legis, quia rectus est. Dulcis, quia perire non patitur; rectus, quia punire non obliviscitur.
segments.en: Now humility may be defined thus: Humility is the virtue by which a man, through a most true knowledge of himself, becomes cheap in his own eyes. This belongs to those who, having set ascents in their hearts, go forward from virtue to virtue, that is from step to step, until they reach the summit of humility, where, set as on Sion—that is, in contemplation—they look upon the truth. For, he says, the lawgiver shall give a blessing (Ps. 83:8): because he who gave the law will also give the blessing; that is, he who commanded humility leads on to truth. And who is this lawgiver but the Lord, sweet and upright, who gave a law to those who fail on the way? (Ps. 24:8.) They fail on the way who abandon the truth. Yet even so, are they abandoned by the sweet Lord? To them, then, the sweet and upright Lord gives the law of the way of humility, by which they may return to the knowledge of truth. He gives a chance of recovering salvation, because he is sweet; yet not without the discipline of the law, because he is upright. Sweet, because he does not suffer them to perish; upright, because he does not forget to punish.

title.la: Quo fructu ascendantur gradus humilitatis
title.en: With what fruit the steps of humility are climbed

segments.la: Hanc itaque legem, qua reditur ad veritatem, beatus Benedictus per duodecim gradus disponit: sicut per decem praecepta legis ac geminam circumcisionem (in quo duodenarius numerus adimpletur) ad Christum venitur; ita his duodecim gradibus ascensis, veritas apprehendatur. Illud quoque quod in scala illa, quae in typo humilitatis Iacob monstrata est, Dominus desuper innixus apparuit (Gen. xxviii, 12, 13), quid nobis aliud innuit, nisi quod in culmine humilitatis constituitur cognitio veritatis?
segments.en: This law, then, by which one returns to truth, blessed Benedict arranges in twelve steps: as one comes to Christ through the ten commandments of the law and the twofold circumcision (in which the number twelve is completed), so, when these twelve steps have been climbed, truth is grasped. That the Lord also appeared leaning from above on that ladder which was shown to Jacob as a type of humility (Gen. 28:12–13)—what else does this hint, except that the knowledge of truth is set at the height of humility?

segments.la: Dominus quippe de summitate scalae prospectiebat super filios hominum tamquam Veritas, cuius oculi sicut fallere nolunt, ita falli non norunt, ut videret si est intelligens aut requirens Deum. An non tibi de alto videtur clamare ac dicere requirentibus se (novit enim qui sunt eius): Transite ad me, omnes qui concupiscitis me, et a generationibus meis implemini? (Eccli. xxiv, 26) et illud: Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego vos reficiam (Matth. xi, 28). Venite, inquit. Quo? Ad me veritatem. Qua? Per humilitatem. Quo fructu? Ego vos reficiam.
segments.en: For the Lord looked down from the top of the ladder upon the sons of men as Truth, whose eyes as they will not deceive, so they cannot be deceived, to see if there were any who understands or seeks God. Does he not seem to you to cry from on high to those who seek him (for he knows who are his): Come over to me, all who desire me, and be filled with my fruits (Sir. 24:26)? And this: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you (Matt. 11:28). Come, he says. Where? To me, the truth. How? By humility. With what fruit? I will refresh you.

segments.la: Sed quae est refectio, quam Veritas ascendentibus promittit, pervenientibus reddit? An forte ipsa est charitas? Ad hanc quippe, ut ait beatus Benedictus, ascensis omnibus humilitatis gradibus monachus mox perveniet (Reg. cap. 7, grad. 12). Vere dulcis et suavis cibus charitas, quae fessos allevat, debiles roborat, maestos laetificat. Iugum denique Veritatis facit suave, et onus leve.
segments.en: But what is this refreshment which Truth promises to those who climb and gives to those who arrive? Is it perhaps charity itself? To this, as blessed Benedict says, the monk will soon come when all the steps of humility have been climbed (Rule, ch. 7, step 12). Truly charity is a sweet and pleasant food, which lifts the weary, strengthens the weak, and gladdens the sad. In short, it makes the yoke of Truth easy and its burden light.

segments.la: Bonus cibus charitas, quae media in ferculo Salomonis consistens (Cantic. iii, 9, 10), diversarum odore virtutum, velut diversi generis fragrantia pigmentorum, esurientes reficit, iucundat reficientes. Ibi siquidem apponitur pax, patientia, benignitas, longanimitas, gaudium in Spiritu sancto; et si quae sunt aliae veritatis seu sapientiae generationes, apparantur in illa.
segments.en: Charity is good food, standing in the midst of Solomon’s litter (Song 3:9–10). By the scent of various virtues, as by the fragrance of spices of different kinds, it refreshes the hungry and delights those who serve. There peace is set out, patience, kindness, long-suffering, joy in the Holy Spirit; and if there are any other offspring of truth or wisdom, they too are served there.

segments.la: Habet et humilitas in eodem ferculo suas epulas, panem scilicet doloris et vinum compunctionis, quas primo Veritas incipientibus offert, quibus utique dicitur: Surgite postquam sederitis, qui manducatis panem doloris (Psal. cxxvi, 2). Habet ibidem contemplatio ex adipe frumenti solidum cibum sapientiae, cum vino quod laetificat cor hominis, ad quae Veritas perfectos invitat, dicens: Comedite, amici mei, et bibite: et inebriamini, charissimi (Cantic. v, 1).
segments.en: Humility also has her dishes on the same platter: the bread of sorrow and the wine of compunction, which Truth first offers to beginners, to whom it is said: Rise after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow (Ps. 126:2). Contemplation there has, from the fat of the wheat, the solid food of wisdom, with the wine that gladdens the heart of man, to which Truth invites the perfect, saying: Eat, my friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved (Song 5:1).

segments.la: Media, inquit, charitate constravit propter filias Ierusalem (ibid. iii, 10); propter imperfectas videlicet animas, quae, dum adhuc solidum cibum minus capere possunt, lacte interim charitatis pro pane, oleo pro vino nutriendae sunt. Quae recte media describitur, quia eius suavitas nec incipientibus praesto est, prohibente timore; nec perfectis satis est, pro abundantiori contemplationis dulcedine. Hi adhuc a noxiis carnalium delectationum humoribus, timoris amarissima potione purgandi, nondum lactis dulcedinem experiuntur: illi iam avulsi a lacte, epulari ab introitu gloriae gloriosius delectantur: solis mediis, id est proficientibus, ita iam melleas quasdam sorbitiunculas charitatis expertis, ut illis interim pro sui teneritudine contenti sint.
segments.en: The midst, he says, he paved with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem (Song 3:10)—that is, for unfinished souls who, while they cannot yet take solid food, must meanwhile be nourished with the milk of charity instead of bread, and with oil instead of wine. It is rightly called the middle course, because its sweetness is not yet at hand for beginners, fear forbidding it, and is not enough for the perfect, because of the more abundant sweetness of contemplation. The first still need to be purged of the noxious humors of fleshly delights by the bitterest draught of fear, and have not yet tasted the sweetness of milk; the last, already weaned from milk, feast more gloriously at the entrance of glory; only those in the middle—those making progress—have already tasted certain honeyed sips of charity, and for the tenderness of their stomachs are content with them for a time.

segments.la: Primus ergo cibus est humilitatis, purgatorius cum amaritudine: secundus charitatis, consolatorius cum dulcedine: tertius contemplationis, solidus cum fortitudine. Heu mihi, Domine Deus virtutum! quousque irasceris super orationem servi tui, cibabis me pane lacrymarum, et potum dabis mihi in lacrymis? Quis me invitabit ad illud vel medium ac dulce charitatis convivium: ubi iusti epulantur in conspectu Dei, et delectantur in laetitia, ut iam non loquens in amaritudine animae meae, dicam Deo: Noli me condemnare: sed epulando in azymis sinceritatis et veritatis, laetus cantem in viis Domini, quoniam magna est gloria Domini? Bona tamen via humilitatis, qua veritas inquiritur, charitas acquiritur, generationes sapientiae participantur. Denique sicut finis legis Christus, sic perfectio humilitatis, cognitio veritatis. Christus cum venit attulit gratiam: Veritas quibus innotuerit, dat charitatem. Innotescit autem humilibus: humilibus ergo dat gratiam.
segments.en: The first food, then, is humility’s, purgative with bitterness; the second, charity’s, consoling with sweetness; the third, contemplation’s, solid with strength. Alas for me, Lord God of hosts! How long will you be angry against the prayer of your servant, feed me with the bread of tears, and give me tears to drink? Who will invite me even to that middle and sweet banquet of charity, where the just feast in the sight of God and delight in gladness, so that I may no longer speak in the bitterness of my soul and say to God, Do not condemn me, but, feasting on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, may sing with joy in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord? Yet good is the way of humility, by which truth is sought, charity is gained, and the fruits of wisdom are shared. In short, as Christ is the end of the law, so the knowledge of truth is the perfection of humility. When Christ came he brought grace; Truth, when it becomes known, gives charity. But it becomes known to the humble: therefore it is to the humble that it gives grace.

title.la: Quo ordine gradus humilitatis ad propositum bravium veritatis perducant; et quomodo Christus per passionem didicit misericordiam
title.en: In what order the steps of humility lead to the prize of truth; and how Christ learned mercy through his Passion

segments.la: Dixi, ut potui, quo fructu humilitatis gradus ascendi debeant: dicam, ut potero, quo ordine ad propositum bravium veritatis perducant. Sed, quia ipsa quoque veritatis agnitio in tribus gradibus consistit, ipsos breviter, si possum, distinguo: quatenus ex hoc clarius innotescat, ad quem trium veritatis duodecimus humilitatis pertingat. Inquirimus namque veritatem in nobis, in proximis, in sui natura. In nobis, nosmetipsos diiudicando; in proximis, eorum malis compatiendo; in sui natura mundo corde contemplando. Observa sicut numerum, ita et ordinem. Primo te doceat Veritas ipsa, quod prius in proximis quam in sui debeat inquiri natura. Post hoc accipies, cur prius in te, quam in proximis inquirere debeas. In numero siquidem beatitudinum, quas suo sermone distinxit Dominus, prius misericordes, quam mundicordes posuit (Matth. v, 7, 8). Misericordes quippe cito in proximis veritatem deprehendunt, dum suos affectus in illos extendunt: dum sic per charitatem se illis conformant, ut illorum vel bona, vel mala, tanquam propria sentiant. Cum infirmis infirmatur, cum scandalizatis uruntur (II Cor. xi, 29). Gaudere cum gaudentibus, flere cum flentibus consueverunt (Rom. xii, 15). Hac charitate fraterna cordis acie mundata, veritatem delectantur in sui contemplari natura, pro cuius amore mala tolerant aliena. Qui vero ita se fratribus non consociant, sed e contrario aut flentibus insultant, aut gaudentibus derogant, dum quod in illis est, in se esse non sentiunt, quia similiter affecti non sunt, veritatem in proximis qualiter deprehendere possunt?
segments.en: I have said, as well as I could, with what fruit the steps of humility ought to be climbed; I will say, as I am able, in what order they lead to the promised prize of truth. But because the recognition of truth itself also consists in three degrees, I distinguish them briefly, if I can, so that it may be clearer to which of the three degrees of truth the twelfth of humility attains. For we seek truth in ourselves, in our neighbors, and in its own nature. In ourselves, by judging ourselves; in our neighbors, by suffering with their evils; in its own nature, by contemplating with a pure heart. Observe the order as well as the number. Let Truth itself first teach you that it ought to be sought in neighbors before it is sought in its own nature. After this you will learn why you ought to seek it in yourself before you seek it in your neighbors. In the number of the Beatitudes which the Lord distinguished in his sermon, he placed the merciful before the pure in heart (Matt. 5:7–8). The merciful quickly catch truth in their neighbors, when they stretch their own feelings toward them, and so conform themselves to them by charity that they feel their goods or ills as their own. They are weak with the weak; they burn with those who are scandalized (2 Cor. 11:29). They have grown used to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15). With the mind’s edge cleansed by this brotherly charity, they delight to contemplate truth in its own nature, for love of which they bear another’s evils. But those who do not so join themselves to their brethren, and instead insult those who weep or belittle those who rejoice—since they do not feel in themselves what is in others, because they are not similarly affected—how can they catch truth in their neighbors?

segments.la: Bene namque convenit illis illud vulgare proverbium: Nescit sanus quid sentiat aeger, aut plenus quid patiatur ieiunus. Et aeger aegro, et ieiunus ieiuno quanto propinquius, tanto familiarius compatiuntur. Sicut enim pura veritas non nisi puro corde videtur, sic miseria fratris verius misero corde sentitur. Sed ut ob alienam miseriam cor miserum habeas, oportet tuam prius agnoscas, ut proximi mentem in tua invenias, et ex te noveris qualiter illi subvenias, exemplo scilicet Salvatoris nostri, qui pati voluit ut compati sciret, miser fieri ut misereri disceret, ut quomodo de ipso scriptum est: Et didicit ex his quae passus est obedientiam (Hebr. v, 8), ita disceret et misericordiam. Non quod ante misereri nesciret, cuius misericordia ab aeterno et usque in aeternum (Psal. cii, 17): sed quod natura sciebat ab aeterno, temporali didicit experimento.
segments.en: The common proverb fits them well: a healthy man does not know what a sick man feels, nor a full man what a fasting man suffers. And the sick sympathize with the sick, and the hungry with the hungry, more nearly and more familiarly the closer they are to that condition. For as pure truth is seen only with a pure heart, so a brother’s misery is more truly felt with a miserable heart. But that you may have a miserable heart for another’s misery, you must first know your own, so that you may find your neighbor’s mind in yours, and know from yourself how to help him—by the example of our Saviour, who willed to suffer that he might know how to suffer with us, to become wretched that he might learn to have mercy; so that, as it is written of him, He learned obedience from the things he suffered (Heb. 5:8), he might in the same way learn mercy. Not that he did not know how to have mercy before—he whose mercy is from eternity to eternity (Ps. 102:17)—but that what he knew by nature from eternity, he learned by experience in time.

segments.la: Sed forte durum tibi videtur, quod dixi Dei sapientiam Christum didicisse misericordiam; quasi is per quem omnia facta sunt, aliquid aliquando ignorasset ex his quae sunt: maxime cum illud quod ex Epistola ad Hebraeos ad id comprobandum commemoravi, alio sensu, qui non ita videatur absurdus, possit intelligi; ut hoc quod dictum est, didicit, non ad ipsum caput referatur in sui persona, sed ad corpus eius, quod est Ecclesia; et sit ita sensus: Et didicit ex his quae passus est obedientiam, hoc est, obedientiam didicit in suo corpore ex his quae passus est in capite. Nam illa mors, illa crux, opprobria, sputa, flagella, quae omnia caput nostrum Christus pertransiit, quid aliud corpori eius, id est nobis, quam praeclara obedientiae documenta fuerunt? Christus enim, ait Paulus, factus est obediens Patri usque ad mortem (Philipp. ii, 8). Qua necessitate? Respondeat apostolus Petrus: Christus passus est pro nobis, vobis relinquens exemplum, ut sequamini, inquit, vestigia eius (I Petr. ii, 21), id est ut imitemini obedientiam eius. Ex his ergo quae passus est, discimus quanta nos, qui puri homines sumus, oporteat pro obedientia perpeti, pro qua is, qui et Deus erat, non dubitaverit mori. Et hoc modo, inquis, inconveniens non erit, si dicitur Christus vel obedientiam, vel misericordiam, seu aliquid aliud in suo corpore didicisse: dum tamen sibi in sua persona nil, quod se ante latuerit, credatur ex tempore potuisse accedere. Sicque ipse sit qui misereri aut obedire doceat, ipse qui discat: quia caput et corpus unus est Christus.
segments.en: But perhaps it seems hard to you that I have said Christ, the Wisdom of God, learned mercy—as if he through whom all things were made had ever been ignorant of anything that is; especially since that which I cited from the Epistle to the Hebrews to prove it can be understood in another sense, which may not seem so absurd: that this word, he learned, is referred not to the Head in his own person, but to his Body, which is the Church; and so the sense would be: He learned obedience from the things he suffered—that is, he learned obedience in his Body from those things which he suffered in the Head. For that death, that cross, those reproaches, spittings, and scourgings, all of which Christ our Head passed through—what else were they to his Body, that is, to us, than noble proofs of obedience? For Christ, says Paul, became obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. 2:8). By what necessity? Let the apostle Peter answer: Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps (1 Pet. 2:21)—that is, that you should imitate his obedience. From the things he suffered, then, we learn how much we who are mere men ought to endure for obedience, for which he who was also God did not hesitate to die. And in this way, you say, it will not be unfitting if Christ is said to have learned obedience, or mercy, or anything else in his Body, provided only it is not believed that anything which had been hidden from him before could have come to him in time in his own person. And so he himself is the one who teaches mercy or obedience, and he himself the one who learns, because Head and Body are one Christ.

segments.la: Non nego hunc intellectum, quin rectus sit: sed ex alio loco ipsius Epistolae, superior interpretatio videtur approbari, ubi dicitur: Nusquam enim angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahae apprehendit: unde debuit per omnia fratribus similari, ut misericors fieret (Hebr. ii, 16, 17). Puto quod haec verba sic ad caput referenda sint, ut corpori penitus aptari non possint. De Verbo utique Dei dictum est quod non angelos apprehendit, hoc est non in unam sibi personam assumpsit, sed semen Abrahae. Neque enim legitur: Verbum angelus factum est, sed: Verbum caro factum est (Ioan. i, 14), et caro de carne Abrahae, iuxta promissionem quae illi primum facta est. Unde, id est ex qua seminis assumptione, debuit per omnia fratribus similari; id est, oportuit ac necesse fuit ut similis nobis passibilis, nostrarum omnia, excepto peccato, genera miseriarum percurreret. Si quaeris, qua necessitate? Ut misericors, inquit, fieret. Et hoc, ais, cur non recte ad corpus referri potest? Sed audi quod paulo post sequitur: In eo enim, in quo passus est ipse et tentatus, potens est et eis qui tentantur auxiliari (Hebr. ii, 18). In quibus verbis quid melius intelligi possit non video; nisi quod ideo pati ac tentari, omnibusque, absque peccato, humanis voluit communicare miseriis (quod est per omnia fratribus similari), ut similiter passis ac tentatis misereri ac compati ipso disceret experimento.
segments.en: I do not deny that this reading is a right one; but from another place in the same Epistle the former interpretation seems to be confirmed, where it is said: For nowhere does he take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham: wherefore he ought to be made like his brethren in all things, that he might become merciful (Heb. 2:16–17). I think these words are so to be referred to the Head that they cannot at all be fitted to the Body. It is said of the Word of God that he did not take hold of angels—that is, he did not assume them into one person with himself—but the seed of Abraham. For we do not read, The Word was made an angel, but The Word was made flesh (John 1:14), and flesh from the flesh of Abraham, according to the promise which was first made to him. Wherefore—that is, from this assumption of the seed—he ought to be made like his brethren in all things: that is, it was fitting and necessary that, passible like us, he should run through all the kinds of our miseries, except sin. If you ask, by what necessity? That he might become merciful, he says. And this, you say, why can it not rightly be referred to the Body? But hear what follows a little after: For in that he himself has suffered and been tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted (Heb. 2:18). In these words I do not see what can better be understood, except that he willed therefore to suffer and to be tempted, and to share in all human miseries except sin (which is to be made like his brethren in all things), that by his own experience he might learn to have mercy and to suffer with those who likewise suffer and are tempted.

segments.la: Quo quidem experimento non dico ut sapientior efficeretur, sed propinquior videretur: quatenus infirmi filii Adam, quos suos fieri et appellari fratres non dedignatus est, suas illi infirmitates committere non dubitarent, qui sanare illas et posset ut Deus, et vellet ut proximus, et cognosceret ut eadem passus. Unde Isaias virum eum appellat dolorum, et scientem infirmitatem (Isa. liii, 3): et Apostolus: Non enim habemus, inquit, pontificem, qui non possit compati infirmitatibus nostris. Unde autem possit, indicans adiungit: Tentatum autem per omnia pro similitudine, absque peccato (Hebr. iv, 15). Beatus quippe Deus, beati Dei Filius, in ea forma, qua non rapinam arbitratus est esse se aequalem Patri, procul dubio impassibilis, priusquam se exinanisset formam servi accipiens (Philipp. ii, 6, 7), sicut miseriam vel subiectionem expertus non erat, sic misericordiam vel obedientiam experimento non noverat. Sciebat quidem per naturam, non autem sciebat per experientiam. At ubi minoratus est non solum a seipso, sed etiam paulo minus ab angelis, qui et ipsi impassibiles sunt per gratiam, non per naturam, usque ad illam formam, in qua pati et subici posset, quod utique (sicut dictum est) in sua non posset; et in passione expertus est misericordiam, et in subiectione obedientiam. Per quam tamen experientiam, non illi (ut dixi) scientia, sed nobis fiducia crevit, dum ex hoc misero genere cognitionis, is a quo longe erraveramus, factus est propior nobis. Quando enim illi appropinquare auderemus, in sua impassibilitate manenti? Nunc autem, Apostolo suadente, monemur cum fiducia adire thronum gratiae ipsius (Hebr. iv, 16), quem nimirum, sicut alibi scriptum est, languores nostros tulisse, et dolores portasse (Isa. liii, 4) cognoscimus, et in eo quo passus est ipse, nobis compati posse non dubitamus.
segments.en: By this experience I do not say that he was made wiser, but that he was seen to be nearer, so that the weak sons of Adam, whom he did not disdain to make and to call his brethren, might not hesitate to commit their infirmities to him who could heal them as God, and would as a neighbor, and knew them as one who had suffered the same. Hence Isaiah calls him a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity (Isa. 53:3); and the Apostle: For we have not a high priest who cannot suffer with our infirmities. And showing whence he can, he adds: But one tempted in all things after our likeness, without sin (Heb. 4:15). For the blessed God, the Son of the blessed God, in that form in which he thought it not robbery to be equal with the Father, was beyond doubt impassible, before he had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). As he had not experienced misery or subjection, so he had not known mercy or obedience by experience. He knew them indeed by nature, but he did not know them by experience. But when he was made lower not only than himself, but even a little lower than the angels, who themselves are impassible by grace, not by nature, even to that form in which he could suffer and be subjected—which, as has been said, he could not in his own—he experienced mercy in the Passion, and obedience in subjection. Yet through this experience, as I have said, not knowledge grew in him, but confidence in us, while by this wretched kind of knowing, he from whom we had wandered far was made nearer to us. For when would we have dared to approach him, remaining in his impassibility? But now, at the Apostle’s urging, we are told to come with confidence to the throne of his grace (Heb. 4:16), whom we know, as it is written elsewhere, to have borne our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isa. 53:4), and we do not doubt that he can suffer with us in that in which he himself has suffered.

segments.la: Non ergo debet absurdum videri, si dicitur Christum non quidem aliquid scire coepisse, quod aliquando nescierit; scire tamen alio modo misericordiam ab aeterno per divinitatem, et aliter in tempore didicisse per carnem. Vide ne et simili locutionis modo illud dictum sit, quod Dominus requirentibus discipulis de die ultimo se nescire respondit. Nam quomodo diem illum ille nesciebat, in quo omnes thesauri sapientiae et scientiae thesauri sunt absconditi? (Coloss. ii, 3.) Cur ergo se scire negabat, quod certum est quia nescire non poterat? Numquid forte mendaciter eis voluit celare, quod utiliter non valuit innotescere? Absit. Sicut nil ignorare poterat, cum sapientia sit, sic nec mentiri, cum veritas sit. Sed volens discipulos ab inutilis inquisitionis curiositate compescere, quod inquirebant se scire negavit: non omni modo quidem, sed tali quodam modo, quo negare veraciter potuit. Nam etsi suae divinitatis intuitu aequae omnia, praeterita scilicet, praesentia atque futura perlustrando, diem quoque illum palam habebat; non tamen ullis carnis suae sensibus experiendo agnoverat. Alioquin iam spiritu oris sui Antichristum interfecerat, iam auribus sui corporis archangelum vociferantem, et tubam sonantem, in quo strepitu mortui suscitandi sunt, audierat: iam oculis suae carnis oves haedosque, qui ab invicem segregandi sunt, perspexerat.
segments.en: Therefore it ought not to seem absurd if it is said, not that Christ began to know something which he had at some time not known, but that he knows mercy in one way from eternity through the Godhead, and learned it in another way in time through the flesh. See whether it was not in a similar manner of speaking that the Lord, when the disciples asked about the last day, answered that he did not know. For how did he not know that day, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2:3)? Why then did he deny that he knew what it is certain he could not not-know? Did he perhaps wish to hide it from them with a lie, because he could not usefully make it known? God forbid. As he could be ignorant of nothing, since he is Wisdom, so he could not lie, since he is Truth. But wishing to check the disciples’ curiosity of useless inquiry, he denied that he knew what they asked—not in every way, but in a certain way in which he could deny it truthfully. For although by the gaze of his Godhead, surveying all things equally, past, present, and future, he had that day openly before him, he had not yet come to know it by experiencing it with any senses of his flesh. Otherwise he would already have slain Antichrist with the breath of his mouth; would already have heard with the ears of his body the archangel crying out and the trumpet sounding, at which noise the dead are to be raised; would already have seen with the eyes of his flesh the sheep and the goats who are to be separated from one another.

segments.la: Denique ut intelligas, quod illa tantum cognitione, quae per carnem fit, se illum diem nescire perhibuerit, vigilanter respondens, non ait: Nec ego scio, sed: Nec ipse, inquit, Filius hominis scit (Marc. xiii, 32). Quid est Filius hominis, nisi nomen assumptae carnis? Quo siquidem nomine intelligi datur, quia dicens se aliquid nescire, non iuxta quod Deus est, sed secundum hominem loquitur. Alias quippe loquens de se secundum suam deitatem, non Filium vel Filium hominis, sed Ego, vel Me, saepius ponere consuevit, ut ibi: Amen, amen dico vobis, antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum (Ioan. viii, 58). Ego sum, ait, non: Filius hominis est. Nec dubium quin de illa essentia diceret, qua ante Abraham et sine initio est, non qua post Abraham et ex Abraham factus est. Alibi quoque hominum de se opinionem a discipulis inquirens, Quem dicunt, inquit, homines esse, non « me », sed Filium hominis? Rursus eosdem interrogans, quid de se ipsi quoque sentirent: Vos autem, non « quem Filium hominis », sed quem me, ait, esse dicitis? Carnalis videlicet populi sententiam de carne inquirens, nomen carnis, quod proprie est Filius hominis, posuit: spirituales vero discipulos de sua divinitate interrogans, non Filium hominis, sed signanter me dixit. Quod denique Petrus intelligens, quid per hoc quod dixerat, me, requisiti fuissent, sua responsione aperuit: Tu es, inquiens, non « Iesus filius Virginis », sed Christus Filius Dei. Quod utique si respondisset, nihilominus veritatem dixisset; sed in verbis interrogationis sensum interrogantis prudenter advertens, competenter proprieque ad interrogata respondit, dicens: Tu es Christus, Filius Dei.
segments.en: Finally, that you may understand that he claimed not to know that day only by that knowledge which comes through the flesh, he answered watchfully, and did not say, “Nor do I know,” but, Nor does the Son of Man himself know (Mark 13:32). What is “Son of Man” if not the name of the assumed flesh? By that name it is given to be understood that when he says he does not know something, he is speaking not according to what he is as God, but according to man. Elsewhere, when speaking of himself according to his Godhead, he was accustomed to put not “the Son” or “the Son of Man,” but I or me, as there: Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham was made, I am (John 8:58). I am, he says, not “the Son of Man is.” There is no doubt he was speaking of that essence by which he is before Abraham and without beginning, not of that by which he was made after Abraham and from Abraham. Elsewhere also, asking the disciples men’s opinion of him, he says, Whom do men say—not “that I”—but that the Son of Man is? Again, asking the same men what they themselves thought of him: But whom do you say—not “that the Son of Man is”—but that I am? Inquiring, that is, the carnal people’s view of the flesh, he put the name of the flesh, which properly is Son of Man; but questioning the spiritual disciples about his Godhead, he did not say “Son of Man,” but pointedly me. Peter, understanding what they were being asked by this word me, opened it in his reply: You are, he says, not “Jesus, son of the Virgin,” but Christ, the Son of God. Had he given the former answer, he would still have spoken the truth; but wisely noticing in the words of the question the sense of the one who asked, he answered the thing asked fitly and properly: You are the Christ, the Son of God.

segments.la: Cum igitur videas Christum in una quidem persona duas habere naturas, unam qua semper fuit, alteram qua esse coepit; et secundum sempiternum quidem suum esse, semper omnia nosse, secundum temporale vero, multa temporaliter expertum fuisse: cur fateri dubitas, ut esse in tempore coepit in carne, sic carnis quoque miserias scire coepisse, illo dumtaxat modo cognitionis, quem docet defectio carnis? Quod utique genus scientiae Protoplasti sapientius feliciusque nescirent, quando ad attingere nisi stulte misereque non poterant. Sed plasmator eorum Deus requirens quod perierat, opus suum miseratus prosecutus est, descendens et ipse misericorditer, quo illi ceciderant miserabiliter. Voluit experiri in se quod illi faciendo contra se merito paterentur, non simili quidem curiositate, sed mirabili charitate: non ut miser cum miseris remaneret, sed ut misericors factus miseros liberaret. Factus, inquam, misericors, non illa misericordia, quam felix manens habuit ab aeterno, sed quam mediante miseria reperit in habitu nostro. Porro pietatis opus, quod per illam coepit, in ista perfecit: non quod sola illa non posset perficere, sed quia nobis non potuit absque ista sufficere. Utraque siquidem necessaria, sed nobis haec magis congrua fuit. O ineffabilis pietatis excogitatio! Quando illam adverteremus incognitam nobis compassionem, quae non passione praeventa, cum impassibilitate perdurat? Attamen si illa quae miseriam nescit, misericordia non praecessisset, ad hanc, cuius miseria mater est, non accessisset. Si non accessisset, non attraxisset; si non attraxisset, non extraxisset. Unde autem extraxit, nisi de lacu miseriae, et de luto faecis? (Psal. xxxix, 3.) Nec illam tamen misericordiam deseruit, sed hanc inseruit; non mutavit, sed multiplicavit, sicut scriptum est: Homines et iumenta salvabis, Domine, quemadmodum multiplicasti misericordiam tuam, Deus (Psal. xxxv, 7, 8).
segments.en: When therefore you see that Christ has two natures in one person, one by which he always was, the other by which he began to be; and that according to his everlasting being he always knew all things, but according to his temporal being he experienced many things in time: why do you hesitate to confess that, as he began in time to exist in the flesh, so he also began to know the miseries of the flesh—at least by that mode of knowing which the weakness of the flesh teaches? This kind of knowledge our first parents would more wisely and more happily have not known, since they could reach it only foolishly and wretchedly. But God their maker, seeking what had perished, in mercy followed his own work, himself descending mercifully to where they had fallen miserably. He willed to experience in himself what they deservedly suffered by acting against him—not with a curiosity like theirs, but with wondrous charity: not that he might remain wretched with the wretched, but that, having become merciful, he might set the wretched free. Become merciful, I say—not with that mercy which he, remaining blessed, had from eternity, but with that which, by the medium of misery, he found in our condition. Further, the work of tenderness which he began by the former, he completed in the latter: not that the former alone could not complete it, but because without the latter it could not suffice for us. Both were necessary, but this latter was more fitted to us. O unspeakable device of tenderness! When would we have noticed that unknown compassion which, not preceded by suffering, lasts on with impassibility? Yet if that mercy which knows no misery had not gone before, he would not have come to this mercy whose mother is misery. If he had not come, he would not have drawn; if he had not drawn, he would not have drawn out. And from where did he draw out, if not from the pit of misery and the mire of dregs (Ps. 39:3)? Yet he did not abandon that former mercy, but grafted this one in; he did not change it, but multiplied it, as it is written: You will save men and beasts, O Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God (Ps. 35:7–8).

title.la: Primus veritatis gradus est, primum seipsum attendere, seu propriam miseriam agnoscere
title.en: The first degree of truth is first to attend to oneself, or to recognize one’s own misery

segments.la: Sed iam ad propositum redeamus. Si ergo se miserum fecit, qui miser non erat, ut experiretur quod et ante sciebat, quanto magis tu, non dico ut te facias quod non es, sed ut attendas quod es, quia vere miser es, et sic discas misereri, qui hoc aliter scire non potes? Ne forte si proximi malum consideres, et tuum non attendas, movearis non ad miserationem, sed ad indignationem; non ad adiuvandum, sed ad iudicandum; denique non ad instruendum in spiritu lenitatis, sed ad destruendum in spiritu furoris. Vos, qui spirituales estis, ait Apostolus, huiusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis. Apostoli consilium sive etiam praeceptum est, ut mansueto, id est eo spiritu fratri aegrotanti subvenias, quo tibi vis subveniri cum aegrotas. Et ut scias qualiter erga delinquentem mansuescere possis, Considerans, inquit, teipsum, ne et tu tenteris (Galat. vi, 1).
segments.en: But let us now return to our purpose. If then he made himself wretched who was not wretched, that he might experience what he already knew, how much more should you—I do not say make yourself what you are not, but attend to what you are, because you are truly wretched—and so learn to pity, which otherwise you cannot know? Otherwise, if you consider your neighbor’s evil and do not attend to your own, you may be moved not to compassion but to indignation; not to help but to judge; in short, not to instruct in the spirit of gentleness, but to destroy in the spirit of wrath. You who are spiritual, says the Apostle, instruct such a one in the spirit of gentleness. It is the Apostle’s counsel, even his command, that you come to the aid of a sick brother with that meek spirit in which you wish to be aided when you are sick. And that you may know how you can grow meek toward one who fails: Considering yourself, he says, lest you also be tempted (Gal. 6:1).

segments.la: Considerare libet, quam bene discipulus Veritatis ordinem sequatur Magistri. In beatitudinibus, quas supra memoravi, sicut prius misericordes quam mundicordes, sic prius mites quam misericordes pronuntiati sunt (Matth. v, 4, 7, 8). Et Apostolus cum spirituales hortaretur ad instruendum carnales, adiunxit, in spiritu lenitatis. Instructio quippe fratrum pertinet ad misericordes; spiritus lenitatis, ad mites. Ac si diceret: Inter misericordes deputari non potest, qui in semetipso mitis non est. Ecce Apostolus aperte ostendit, quod superius me ostensurum promisi, prius videlicet veritatem inquirendam esse in nobis quam in proximis: considerans, inquiens, teipsum, hoc est, quam facilis ad tentandum, quam pronus ad peccandum, quatenus ex tui consideratione mitescas, sicque ad succurrendum aliis in spiritu lenitatis accedas. Alioquin si monentem non audis Discipulum, arguentem time Magistrum: Hypocrita, eiice primum trabem de oculo tuo, et sic videbis festucam eiicere de oculo fratris tui (Matth. vii, 5).
segments.en: It is worth considering how well the disciple of Truth follows the Master’s order. In the Beatitudes I recalled above, as the merciful are named before the pure in heart, so the meek are named before the merciful (Matt. 5:4, 7, 8). And the Apostle, when he exhorted the spiritual to instruct the carnal, added, in the spirit of gentleness. Instruction of the brethren belongs to the merciful; the spirit of gentleness, to the meek. As if he said: He cannot be counted among the merciful who is not meek in himself. See, the Apostle clearly shows what I promised above to show: that truth must be sought in ourselves before it is sought in our neighbors. Considering yourself, he says—that is, how easy you are to tempt, how prone to sin—so that by considering yourself you may grow meek, and so come to help others in the spirit of gentleness. Otherwise, if you will not hear the Disciple warning, fear the Master rebuking: Hypocrite, cast out first the beam from your own eye, and then you shall see to cast out the mote from your brother’s eye (Matt. 7:5).

segments.la: Trabes in oculo grandis et grossa, superbia in mente est, quae quadam corpulentia sui vana, non sana; tumida, non solida, oculum mentis obscurat, veritatem obumbrat: ita ut si tuam occupaverit mentem, iam tu te videre, iam te talem, qualis es, vel qualis esse potes, non possis sentire, sed qualem te amas, talem te vel putes esse, vel speres fore. Quid enim aliud est superbia, quam ut quidam sanctus definit, amor propriae excellentiae? Unde et nos possumus dicere, per contrarium, humilitatem propriae excellentiae esse contemptum. Amor vero, sicut nec odium, veritatis iudicium nescit. Vis iudicium Veritatis audire? Sicut audio, sic iudico: non sicut odi, non sicut amo, non sicut timeo. Est iudicium odii, ut illud: Nos legem habemus, et secundum legem nostram debet mori (Ioan. xix, 7). Est et timoris, ut illud: Si dimittimus eum sic, venient Romani, et tollent nostrum locum et gentem (Ioan. xi, 48). Iudicium vero amoris, ut David de filio parricida: Parcite, inquit, puero Absalon (II Reg. xviii, 5). Et legibus humanis statutum, et in causis tam ecclesiasticis quam saecularibus servatum scio, speciales amicos causantium non debere admitti ad iudicium: ne vel fallant, vel fallantur amore suorum. Quod si culpam amici tuo iudicio amor illius aut minuit, aut prorsus abscondit, quanto magis amor tui tuum contra te iudicium fallit?
segments.en: The beam in the eye, large and thick, is pride in the mind, which by a certain vain, not healthy, bulk of itself—swollen, not solid—darkens the mind’s eye and overshadows the truth. So if it occupies your mind, you can no longer see yourself, no longer feel yourself to be such as you are, or such as you can be, but you either think you are, or hope you will be, such as you love to be. For what else is pride than, as a certain holy man defines it, the love of one’s own excellence? Hence we too can say, by contrast, that humility is the contempt of one’s own excellence. But love, like hatred, does not know the judgment of truth. Do you wish to hear the judgment of Truth? As I hear, so I judge: not as I hate, not as I love, not as I fear. There is a judgment of hatred, as this: We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die (John 19:7). There is also one of fear, as this: If we let him alone so, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation (John 11:48). But a judgment of love, as David’s over a parricide son: Spare, he says, the boy Absalom (2 Sam. 18:5). And I know it is laid down by human laws, and kept in both ecclesiastical and secular cases, that the personal friends of the parties should not be admitted to the judgment, lest they deceive or be deceived by love of their own. And if your friend’s love, in your judgment, either lessens his fault or hides it altogether, how much more does love of yourself cheat your judgment against yourself?

segments.la: Qui ergo plene veritatem in se cognoscere curat, necesse est ut, semota trabe superbiae, quae oculum arcet a luce, ascensiones in corde suo disponat, per quas in seipso seipsum inquirat, et sic post duodecimum humilitatis ad primum veritatis gradum pertingat. Cum autem veritate inventa in se, immo se invento in veritate, dicere potuerit: Credidi, propter quod locutus sum; ego autem humiliatus sum nimis: ascendat homo ad cor altum, ut exaltetur veritas, et ad gradum secundum perveniens dicat in excessu suo: Omnis homo mendax. Putas hunc ordinem David non tenuit? Putas hoc Propheta non sensit, quod Dominus, quod Apostolus, quod et nos post ipsos et per ipsos sentimus? Credidi, inquit, Veritati dicenti: Qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris (Ioan. viii, 12). Credidi ergo sequendo, propter quod locutus sum confitendo. Quid confitendo? Veritatem quam cognovi credendo. Postquam autem et credidi ad iustitiam, et locutus sum ad salutem, humiliatus sum nimis, hoc est perfecte. Tamquam diceret: Quia veritatem cognitam in me confiteri contra me non erubui, ad perfectionem humilitatis profeci. Nimis enim pro perfecte potest intelligi, ut ibi: In mandatis eius volet nimis (Psal. cxi, 1). Quod si quis contendat nimis hic pro « valde » positum esse, non pro « perfecte », quia et expositores idipsum videntur astruere, neque hoc discordat a sensu Prophetae. Ut si sentiamus eum dixisse: Ego quidem cum adhuc veritatem non nossem, aliquid me putabam esse, cum nihil essem. At postquam in Christum credendo, id est eius humilitatem imitando, veritatem agnovi, ipsa quidem exaltata est in me ex mea confessione; sed ego humiliatus sum nimis, id est: valde vilui mihi ex mei consideratione.
segments.en: Whoever, then, cares to know the truth fully in himself must, when the beam of pride that shuts the eye from the light has been removed, set ascents in his heart, by which he may search himself out in himself, and so after the twelfth of humility reach the first degree of truth. And when, truth having been found in himself—or rather himself found in the truth—he can say, I believed, therefore I have spoken; but I have been humbled exceedingly, let a man go up to a high heart, that the truth may be exalted, and arriving at the second degree say in his ecstasy, Every man is a liar. Do you think David did not keep this order? Do you think the Prophet did not feel what the Lord, what the Apostle, and what we after them and through them feel? I believed, he says, the Truth who says, He who follows me does not walk in darkness (John 8:12). I believed, therefore, by following, and for that reason I spoke by confessing. Confessing what? The truth I came to know by believing. And after I both believed unto righteousness and spoke unto salvation, I was humbled exceedingly, that is, perfectly. As if he said: Because I was not ashamed to confess against myself the truth I had come to know in myself, I advanced to the perfection of humility. For “exceedingly” can be taken as “perfectly,” as there: He will delight exceedingly in his commandments (Ps. 111:1). And if anyone contends that “exceedingly” is put here for “greatly,” not for “perfectly,” because the expositors also seem to support that, this too is not at odds with the Prophet’s meaning. As if we take him to have said: When I did not yet know the truth, I thought I was something, when I was nothing. But after I recognized the truth by believing in Christ, that is by imitating his humility, the truth was indeed exalted in me by my confession; but I was humbled exceedingly, that is, I became very cheap in my own eyes by considering myself.

title.la: Secundus gradus veritatis est, ex agnitione propriae infirmitatis, compatiri miseriis proximi
title.en: The second degree of truth is, from knowledge of one’s own weakness, to suffer with the miseries of one’s neighbor

segments.la: Humiliatus ergo Propheta in hoc primo gradu veritatis, ut ait in alio psalmo: Et in veritate tua humiliasti me, semetipsum attendat, et ex propria miseria generalem perpendat, sicque ad secundum transiens, dicat in excessu suo: Omnis homo mendax. In quo excessu suo? In illo, procul dubio, quo sese excedens, ac veritati adhaerens, seipsum diiudicat. In illo ergo excessu suo dicat, non indignando aut insultando, sed miserando et compatiendo: omnis homo infirmus, omnis homo miser et impotens, qui nec se, nec alium possit salvare. Sicut dicitur fallax equus ad salutem, non quod equus aliquem fallat, sed quia is seipsum fallit, qui in fortitudine eius confidit: sic omnis homo dicitur mendax, id est fragilis, mutabilis, a quo salus non possit vel sua, vel aliena sperari; quin potius maledictionem incurrat, qui spem suam in homine ponit (Ierem. xvii, 5). Proficiens itaque humilis Propheta per ducatum veritatis, quodque in se lugebat videns in aliis, dum apponit scientiam, apponat et dolorem, ac generaliter, sed veraciter dicat: Omnis homo mendax.
segments.en: The Prophet, then, humbled in this first degree of truth, as he says in another psalm, And in your truth you have humbled me, should attend to himself, and from his own misery weigh the general misery, and so passing to the second degree say in his ecstasy, Every man is a liar. In what ecstasy? In that, no doubt, in which going beyond himself and clinging to truth, he judges himself. In that ecstasy, then, let him say it, not in anger or insult, but in pity and fellow-feeling: every man is weak, every man wretched and powerless, who can save neither himself nor another. As a horse is called deceitful for salvation, not because the horse deceives anyone, but because he deceives himself who trusts in its strength: so every man is called a liar, that is, fragile, changeable, from whom neither his own salvation nor another’s can be hoped; rather he incurs a curse who puts his hope in man (Jer. 17:5). So the humble Prophet, going forward under the guidance of truth, seeing in others what he mourned in himself, as he adds knowledge, let him add sorrow also, and say generally but truly: Every man is a liar.

segments.la: Vide quam longe aliud senserit de se Pharisaeus ille superbus. Quid deprompsit in excessu suo? Deus, gratias ago tibi, quia non sum sicut ceteri hominum (Luc. xviii, 11). Dum in se singulariter exsultat, aliis arroganter insultat. David autem aliter. Ait enim: Omnis homo mendax. Neminem excipit, ne quem decipiat: sciens quia omnes peccaverunt, et omnes egent gloria Dei (Rom. iii, 23). Pharisaeus se solum decipit, quem solum excipit, dum ceteros damnat. Propheta se non excipit a communi miseria, ne excipiatur a misericordia; Pharisaeus exsufflat misericordiam, dum dissimulat miseriam. Propheta affirmat tam de omnibus quam de se: Omnis homo mendax: Pharisaeus confirmat de omnibus praeter se: Non sum, inquiens, sicut ceteri hominum. Et gratias agit, non quia bonus, sed quia solus; non tam de bonis quae habet, quam de malis quae in aliis videt. Nondum de suo trabem eiecerat, et festucas in oculis fratrum enumerat. Nam subdit: Iniusti, raptores (Luc. xviii, 11). Non frustra, ut arbitror, excessum a proposito feci, si utriusque excessus differentiam intellexisti.
segments.en: See how differently that proud Pharisee felt about himself. What did he bring out in his ecstasy? God, I thank you that I am not as the rest of men (Luke 18:11). While he uniquely exults in himself, he arrogantly insults others. David takes another line. For he says: Every man is a liar. He excepts no one, lest he deceive anyone, knowing that all have sinned and all need the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). The Pharisee deceives himself alone, whom alone he excepts while he condemns the rest. The Prophet does not except himself from the common misery, lest he be excepted from mercy; the Pharisee blows mercy away while he conceals misery. The Prophet affirms of all as of himself: Every man is a liar; the Pharisee confirms it of all except himself: I am not, he says, as the rest of men. And he gives thanks not because he is good, but because he is alone; not so much for the goods he has as for the evils he sees in others. He had not yet cast the beam from his own eye, and he counts the motes in his brothers’ eyes. For he adds: Unjust, extortioners (Luke 18:11). I do not think I have gone aside from the subject in vain, if you have understood the difference between these two ecstasies.

segments.la: Iam ad propositum redeundum est. Quos itaque veritas sibi iam innotescere, ac per hoc vilescere fecit, necesse est, si tamen tales se videre cogunt, quales vel se videri erubescunt. Dumque sibi displicet quod sunt, et in se suspirant quod non sunt, quod utique se se fore diffidunt: vehementer sese lugentes id solum consolationis inveniunt, ut seorsum iustitiam, quam sitiunt, usque ad contemptum sui districtissimam a se exigunt satisfactionem, et de cetero emendationem. Sed cum se ad hec insufficientes, imo poene confusos (cum enim fecerint omnia quae mandata fuerint sibi, servos se inutiles dicunt (Luc. xvii, 10)), de iustitia ad misericordiam confugiunt. Et utinam illam consequantur, consilium Veritatis sequuntur: Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur (Matth. v, 7). Et hic est secundus gradus veritatis, quo eam in proximis inquirunt; dum de suis aliorum necessitates exquirunt; dum ex his quae patiuntur, patientibus compati sciunt.
segments.en: We must now return to the matter in hand. Those, then, whom truth has already made known to themselves, and thereby made cheap in their own eyes, must—if they compel themselves to see themselves as they are ashamed even to be seen—when what they are displeases them, and they sigh in themselves for what they are not, which they scarcely trust they will be. Vehemently mourning themselves, they find this only consolation: that they demand from themselves, even to self-contempt, a most strict satisfaction of the justice they thirst for, and amendment for the future. But when they find themselves unequal to this, even almost confounded (for when they have done all that was commanded them, they call themselves unprofitable servants (Luke 17:10)), they flee from justice to mercy. And that they may obtain it, they follow the counsel of Truth: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy (Matt. 5:7). And this is the second degree of truth, in which they seek it in their neighbors, when from their own needs they search out the needs of others, and from what they suffer they know how to suffer with those who suffer.

title.la: Tertius gradus veritatis, mundare oculum cordis ad contemplanda caelestia et divina
title.en: The third degree of truth: to cleanse the eye of the heart for contemplating heavenly and divine things

segments.la: In his ergo tribus quae dicta sunt, id est in luctu paenitentiae, in desiderio iustitiae, in operibus misericordiae si perseverant, a tribus impedimentis, quae contrariantur, ignorantia, aut infirmitate, sui studio contemplationem ad tertium veritatis gradum pertrahent. Hae sunt viae, quae videntur hominibus bonae, illis dumtaxat exceptis, qui laetentur cum male fecerint, et exsultant in rebus pessimis (Prov. ii, 14), ac se de infirmitate vel ignorantia tegunt ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis (Psal. cxl, 4). Sed frustra sibi de infirmitate, vel ignorantia blandiuntur, qui et libenter peccent, libenter ignorent, vel infirmentur. Putas, primo homini profuit, licet ipsum peccatum uxoris, non propriae carnis infirmitatem, defendit (Gen. iii, 12)? aut primi martyris lacrimis, quorum aures suas continuerunt (Act. vii, 56), per ignorantiam excusabiles erunt? Qui igitur studio et amore peccandi a veritate se sentiunt alienatos, infirmitate et ignorantia prorsus: studium in gemitum, amorem in moerorem convertant, infirmitatem carnis fervore iustitiae vincent, ignorantiam liberalitate repleant: ne si nunc gementem, mandant, si infirmum veritatis, ignorantem, campotestate magna et virtute venientem, terrentem, arguentem, sese cum rubore cognoscant, frustra eum tunc tempore respondeant: Quando te vidimus egere, et non ministravimus tibi? (Matth. xxv, 44.) Cogneoscetur certe tunc iudex misericordiae (Iac. ii, 13), quia eum ignoratur misericordiam quaerens. Denique videntur in quem transfixerunt (Ioan. xix, 37): similiter et avari quem contempserunt. Ab omni ergo labe, infirmitate, ignorantia studiove contracta, flendo, iustitiam esuriendo, operibus misericordiae insistendo, mundatur oculus cordis, cui se in sui puritate Veritas videndam promittit: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt (Matth. v, 8). Sunt sibi itaque hi gradus, sicut praediximus, ut primum ascendimus per laborem humilitatis, ad secundum per affectum compassionis, ad tertium per excessum contemplationis. In primo veritas recipitur severe; in secundo, pia; in tertio, pura. In primo nos percutit, qui in nobis sumus; in secundo dum affectu perducit, quo aliis miseremu; ad tertium purius rapit, qui ad invisibilia sublevamur.
segments.en: If therefore in these three things that have been named—in the mourning of penitence, in the desire of justice, in the works of mercy—they persevere, they will draw contemplation, from the three hindrances that fight against it (ignorance, weakness, and self-will), up to the third degree of truth. These are ways that seem good to men—excepting only those who are glad when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. 2:14), and cover themselves with weakness or ignorance to make excuses in sins (Ps. 140:4). From every stain contracted by weakness, ignorance, or will, the eye of the heart is cleansed by weeping, by hungering for justice, by clinging to works of mercy: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matt. 5:8). We first ascend by the labor of humility, to the second by the affection of compassion, to the third by the ecstasy of contemplation.

title.la: Quomodo sancta Trinitas hos tres veritatis gradus in nobis operetur
title.en: How the Holy Trinity works these three degrees of truth in us

segments.la: Interlucet hic mihi mira quaedam ac divisa individuae Trinitatis operatio, si quo modo tamen ab homine sciente in speculo ineffabilis illa possit capi cooperantium sibi personarum divisio. In primo si quidem gradus Filius, in secundo Spiritus sanctus, in tertio mihi Pater operari videtur. Vis audire Filii operationem? Si ego, inquit, lavi vos pedes Dominus et magister, et vos debetis alter alterius lavare pedes? (Ioan. xiii, 14, 15.) Tradidit discipulis humilitatis formam veritatis. Magister quis in primo gradu primum eis veritatem innotescere. At deinde et ipsius Spiritus sancti: Charitas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis (Rom. v, 5). Charitas quippe Donum est Spiritus sancti, qua fit ut qui sub disciplina Filii per humilitatem ad primum veritatis gradum iam profecerunt, ad secundum per compassionem proximi, sub magisterio Spiritus sancti perveniant. Audi et de Patre. Beatus es, Simon Bar Iona, quia caro et sanguis non revelavit tibi, sed Pater meus qui est in caelis (Matth. xvi, 17). Confiteor tibi,
segments.en: Here a certain wondrous and distinct working of the undivided Trinity shines through to me, if that ineffable distinction of the Persons cooperating can in any way be grasped by a man who knows in a mirror. In the first degree the Son seems to me to work, in the second the Holy Spirit, in the third the Father. Do you wish to hear the Son’s working? If I, he says, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet (John 13:14–15). The Master handed the disciples the form of the humility of truth, that in the first degree truth might first become known to them. And then of the Holy Spirit himself: The charity of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us (Rom. 5:5). Charity is the Gift of the Holy Spirit, by which those who under the Son’s discipline have already advanced by humility to the first degree of truth come, under the Spirit’s teaching, to the second by compassion for the neighbor. Hear also of the Father. Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matt. 16:17).

segments.la: Pater, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus, et revelasti ea parvulis (Matth. xi, 25). Vides quia quos verbo et exemplo prius Filius humiliavit, super quos deinde Spiritus sanctus charitatem effudit, hos tandem in gloria Pater recepit? Filius facit discipulos, Paraclitus consolatur amicos, Pater exaltat filios. Quia vero non solum Filius, sed et Pater et Spiritus sanctus veraciter Veritas appellantur; constat quod una eademque Veritas, servata proprietate personarum, tria haec in tribus gradibus operatur. Primo scilicet instruit, ut magister; secundo consolatur, ut amicus; vel frater; tertio astringit, ut filios pater.
segments.en: Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and have revealed them to little ones (Matt. 11:25). Do you see that those whom the Son first humbled by word and example, upon whom the Holy Spirit then poured out charity, the Father at last receives in glory? The Son makes disciples, the Paraclete consoles friends, the Father exalts sons. And because not only the Son, but also the Father and the Holy Spirit are truly called Truth, it is clear that one and the same Truth, the property of the Persons being kept, works these three things in the three degrees. First it instructs, as master; second it consoles, as friend or brother; third it binds, as a father his sons.

segments.la: Dei quippe Filius, Verbum scilicet ac sapientia Patris, primum quidem illam animam carne depressam, peccato captivam, ignorantia caecam, exterioribus deditam; elementer assumens, potenter erigens, prudenter instruens, introrsum trahens, ac mirabiliter uniens tanquam pro se vicariam, ipse sibi iudicem statuit, ita ut pro reverentia Verbi cui coniungitur, ipsa sui accusatrix, testis, et iudex, contra se Veritatis fungatur officio. Ex qua prima coniunctione Verbi et rationis humilitas nascitur. Aliam deinde partem, quae dicitur voluntas, veneno quidem carnis infectam, sed iam ratione discussam, Spiritus sanctus dignanter visitans, suaviter pugnans, ardenter afficiens, misericordem facit: ita ut mox pellis quae uncta extenditur, ipsa quoque unctione perfusa consuescat usque ad inimicos per affectum dilatari. Et sic ex hac secunda coniunctione Spiritus Dei et voluntatis humanae, charitas efficitur. Utramque vero partem: rationem scilicet et voluntatem, alteram vero veritatis instructam, alteram spiritus veritatis afflatam; illam bysso humilitatis aspersam, hanc nive charitatis successam; tandem iam perfectam animam, propter humilitatem sine macula, propter charitatem sine ruga; cum nec voluntas rationi repugnat, nec ratio veritatem dissimulat, gloriosam sibi sponsam Pater conglutinat: ita ut nec ratio de se, nec voluntas de proximo cogitare sinatur, sed hoc solum beata illa anima dicere delectetur, Introduxit me Rex in cubiculum suum. Digna certe, quae de schola humilitatis (in qua primum sub magistro Filio ad seipsam intrare didicit, iuxta commontionem ad se factam, Si ignoras te, egredere et pasce haedos tuos (Cantic. i, 3, 7)) digna ergo, quae de schola illa humilitatis doce Spiritus sanctus in cellaria charitatis (cuius amor proximorum pectora intelligenda sunt) per affectionem introduceretur; unde suffulta floribus, ac stipata malis, bonis scilicet moribus et virtutibus sanctis, ad Regis demum cubiculum, cuius amor angusti, admitteretur. Ibi modicum, hora videlicet quasi dimidia, silentio facto in caelo, inter desideratos amplexus suaviter quiescens, ipsa quidem dormit, sed cor eius vigilat, quo utique interim veritatis arcana rimatur: quorum postmodum memori stamim se reditura pascatur. Ibi videt invisibilia, audit in-
segments.en: For the Son of God, the Word and Wisdom of the Father, first takes that soul pressed down by flesh, captive to sin, blind with ignorance, given to outward things; and raising it, teaching it, drawing it inward, and wondrously uniting it as a vicar for himself, he sets it as judge over itself, so that out of reverence for the Word to which it is joined it becomes its own accuser, witness, and judge, and serves the office of Truth against itself. From this first joining of the Word and reason, humility is born. Then the Holy Spirit visits the other part, called the will—infected by the poison of the flesh, but already sifted by reason—and by fighting sweetly and kindling it makes it merciful, so that the skin anointed is stretched, and by that anointing learns to be dilated even toward enemies. And so from this second joining of the Spirit of God and the human will, charity is made. Then both parts—reason instructed by truth, will breathed upon by the Spirit of truth; the one sprinkled with the linen of humility, the other kindled with the snow of charity—the Father joins to himself as a glorious bride, without spot because of humility, without wrinkle because of charity. Then that blessed soul delights to say only this: The King has brought me into his chamber.

title.la: Gradus iidem in raptu sancti Pauli declarantur
title.en: The same degrees are shown in the rapture of St. Paul

segments.la: Putas, hos gradus sanctus Paulus non transierat, qui usque ad tertium caelum se raptum fuisse testatur? (II Cor. xii, 2.) Sed quare raptum, et non potius ductum? Ut videlicet in hoc discas Apostolum non se dicit fuisse, quo nec ductus scivit, nec ductus potuit ire: me, qui procul dubio minor sum Paulo, ad tertium caelum nulla mea virtute, nullo meo labore pervenire posse praesumam: ne vel de virtute confidam, pro labore diffidam. Qui enim ad locum tur aut ducitur, ex quo ipso quod docentem vel ducentem sequitur, labore convinctur, et aliquid ex se agit, ut ad destinatum locum vel sensum pertrahatur, ita ut dicere possit: Non autem ego, sed gratia Dei mecum (I Cor. xv, 10). Qui vero rapitur, non suis viribus, sed alienis innixus, tamquam nescius quocumque portatur, nec de toto ia se, nec de parte gloriatur, ubi nec per se, nec cum alio aliquid operatus. Ad primum itaque sive ad medium caelum ductus vel adiutus Apostolus ascendere potuit: ad tertium autem ut perveniret, rapi oportuit. Nam ut hoc et Filius legitur descendisse, ut vocaret et iuvaret ascensuros ad primum: et Spiritus sanctus missus fuisse, qui perduceret ad secundum. Pater vero, sicut Filio et Spiritui sancto semper cooperatur, nunquam tamen aut de caelo descendisse, aut nunquam legiter missus fuisse. Lego certe, quod misericordia Domini plena est terra (Psal. xxxii, 5); et, Pleni sunt caeli et terra gloria tua, et multa huiusmodi. Lego et de Filio, Postquam venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum (Galat. iv, 4). Et ipse Filius loquitur de se, Spiritus Domini misit me (Isa. lxi, 1). Et per eumdem prophetam: Et nunc, inquit, Dominus misit me et Spiritus eius (Isa. xlviii, 16). Lego et de Spiritu sancto, Paraclitus autem Spiritus sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo (Ioan. xiv, 26). Et, Cum assumptus fuero, mittam vobis eum (Ioan. xvi, 7), haud dubium quin Spiritum sanctum. Patrem autem in sua persona, licet nusquam non sit, nusquam tamen invenio nisi in caelis, ut in Evangelio, Et Pater meus qui est in caelis (Matth. xviii, 10); et in oratione, Pater noster qui es in caelis (Matth. vi, 9).
segments.en: Do you suppose St. Paul had not passed through these degrees, who testifies that he was caught up as far as the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2)? But why caught up, and not rather led? That you may learn from this that the Apostle does not say he went where he neither knew the way as one led, nor could go as one led—so that I, who am doubtless less than Paul, may not presume to reach the third heaven by any virtue or labor of my own: lest I trust in virtue, or despair because of labor. For he who is led follows a teacher and does something of himself, so that he can say, Yet not I, but the grace of God with me (1 Cor. 15:10). But he who is caught up is carried, leaning not on his own powers but on another’s, as one who does not know, and cannot boast. To the first or middle heaven the Apostle could ascend led or helped; but to reach the third he had to be caught up. For the Son is read to have descended, that he might call and help those who would climb to the first; and the Holy Spirit to have been sent, that he might lead to the second. The Father, though he always cooperates with the Son and the Holy Spirit, is never read to have descended from heaven or to have been sent. The Father I find in his own person nowhere except in the heavens: My Father who is in heaven (Matt. 18:10); Our Father who art in heaven (Matt. 6:9).

segments.la: Unde nimirum colligo, quod quia Pater non descendit, Apostolus, ut eum videret, ad tertium caelum ascendere quidem non potuit, quo tamen se raptum memoravit. Denique, Nemo ascendit in caelum, nisi qui descendit de caelo Filius hominis (Ioan. iii, 13). Et ne putes de primo dictum vel secundo, dicit tibi David: A summo caelo egressio eius (Psal. xviii, 7). Ad quod iterum non subito raptus, non furtim sublatus, sed, Videntibus, inquit, illis, id est Apostolis, elevatus est (Act. i, 9). Non sicut Elias, qui unum (IV Reg. ii, 11); non sicut Paulus, qui nullum (vix enim vel seipsum testem aut arbitrum habere potuit, ipso perhibente, Nescio, Deus scit (II Cor. xii, 2)): sed ut Omnipotens, qui quando voluit descendit, quando voluit ascendit, pro suo arbitrio arbitros et spectatores, locum et tempus, diem et horam exspectans, videntibus illis, quos scilicet tanta visione dignatur, elevatus est. Raptus est Paulus, raptus est Elias, translatus est Enoch (Eccli. xliv, 16): Redemptor vero noster legitur elevatus, hoc est, ex seipso levatus, non aliunde adiutus. Denique non currus vehiculo, non angeli adminiculo, sed propria virtute subnixum suscepit eum nubes ab oculis eorum (Act. i, 9). Cur hoc? An fessum iuvit? an pigrum impulit? an cadentem sustinuit? Absit. Sed suscepit eum ab oculis carnalibus discipulorum: qui, etsi Christum noverant secundum carnem, sed ultra iam non noscerent. Quos ergo per humilitatem ad primum caelum Filius vocat, hos in secundo per charitatem Spiritus aggregat, ad tertium per contemplationem Pater exaltat. Primo humiliantur in veritate, et dicunt, In veritate tua humiliasti me (Psal. cxviii, 75). Secundo congaudent veritati, et psallunt, Ecce quam bonum, et quam iucundum habitare fratres in unum (Psal. cxxxii, 1). De charitate quippe scriptum est, Congaudet autem veritati (I Cor. xiii, 6). Tertio ad arcana veritatis rapiuntur, et aiunt, Secretum meum mihi, secretum meum mihi (Isa. xxiv, 16).
segments.en: From this I gather that because the Father did not descend, the Apostle, in order to see him, could not climb to the third heaven, though he recorded that he was caught up there. Finally, No one has ascended into heaven except him who descended from heaven, the Son of Man (John 3:13). And lest you think this said of the first or second heaven, David says to you: His going forth is from the highest heaven (Ps. 18:7). To that he was not suddenly caught up, not secretly taken up, but, While they looked on, he says—that is, the Apostles—he was lifted up (Acts 1:9). Not like Elijah, who had one witness (2 Kings 2:11); not like Paul, who had none (for he could hardly have even himself as witness or judge, himself declaring, I know not, God knows (2 Cor. 12:2)): but as the Almighty, who descended when he willed and ascended when he willed, waiting at his own choice for witnesses and spectators, place and time, day and hour, was lifted up while they looked on, whom he thought worthy of so great a vision. Paul was caught up, Elijah was caught up, Enoch was translated (Sir. 44:16): but our Redeemer is read to have been lifted up, that is, raised by himself, not helped from elsewhere. Finally, not by the vehicle of a chariot, not by the aid of an angel, but a cloud received him, resting on his own power, from their eyes (Acts 1:9). Why this? Did it help him as one weary? did it urge him as one slow? did it hold him as one falling? Far from it. But it received him from the bodily eyes of the disciples: who, though they had known Christ according to the flesh, would now know him so no longer. Those therefore whom the Son calls through humility to the first heaven, the Spirit gathers in the second through charity, the Father exalts to the third through contemplation. First they are humbled in the truth, and say, In your truth you have humbled me (Ps. 118:75). Second they rejoice with the truth, and sing, Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell in one (Ps. 132:1). For of charity it is written, It rejoices with the truth (1 Cor. 13:6). Third they are caught up to the secrets of truth, and say, My secret to myself, my secret to myself (Isa. 24:16).

title.la: Gemitus et suspiria sancti Bernardi, ad Veritatem anhelantis
