title.en: The sighs of St. Bernard, panting toward the Truth

segments.la: Sed quid ego miser, superflua magis loquacitate quam spiritus vivacitate, duos caelos superiores percurro, qui manibus pedibusque repens adhuc sub inferiore laboro? Ad quod tamen iam, ipso iuvante, quo et vocante, mihi scalam erexi. Illic siquidem iter est, quo ostendat mihi salutare Dei. Iam Dominum desuper innixum suspicio, iam ad vocem veritatis exsulto. Vocavit me, et ego respondi illi: Operi manuum tuarum porriges dexteram (Iob xiv, 15). Tu quidem, Domine, gressus meos dinumeras, sed ego lentus ascensor, fessus viator, diverticula quaero. Vae mihi, si tenebrae me comprehendant, aut si mea fuga fiat in hieme, vel in sabbato: dum nunc ad lucem, cum tempus acceptabile et dies salutis sunt, proficisci dissimulo. Quid moror? Ora pro me, fili, frater, socie, et particeps profectus mei, si quis est, in Domino. Ora omnipotentem, quatenus sic pigrum roboret pedem, ut tamen non veniat mihi pes superbiae. Etsi enim pes piger, ut ad veritatis gradum ascendat, idoneus non est: tolerabilior tamen est isto, qui in ea stare non potest, ut habes ibi: Expulsi sunt, nec potuerunt stare (Psal. xxxv, 12, 13).
segments.en: But why do I, a poor man, with superfluous talkativeness rather than liveliness of spirit, run over the two higher heavens, I who still labor under the lower one, crawling on hands and feet? Yet already, with the help of him who also calls me, I have set up a ladder for myself to that place. There indeed is the way, that he may show me the salvation of God. Already I look up to the Lord leaning from above; already I exult at the voice of truth. He called me, and I answered him: You will stretch your right hand to the work of your hands (Job 14:15). You indeed, Lord, number my steps, but I am a slow climber, a tired traveler, and I look for by-paths. Woe to me if darkness overtake me, or if my flight be in winter or on the Sabbath, while I still put off setting out toward the light, now that it is the acceptable time and the day of salvation. Why do I delay? Pray for me, son, brother, companion, and sharer of my going forward, if anyone is, in the Lord. Pray the Almighty that he so strengthen my slow foot that the foot of pride may not come to me. For though a slow foot is not fit to climb the degree of truth, it is still more tolerable than that one which cannot stand in it, as you have there: They were cast out, and they could not stand (Ps. 35:12–13).

segments.la: Et hoc quidem de superbis. Sed quid de illorum capite? quid de illo, qui dicitur rex super omnes filios superbiae? (Iob xli, 25.) Et ipse, inquit, in veritate non stetit (Ioan. viii, 44): et alibi, Videbam Satanam sicut fulgur cadentem de caelo (Luc. x, 18). Quare hoc, nisi propter superbiam? Vae mihi, si et me viderit, qui alta a longe cognoscit, superbientem; et illam in me terribilem intonet vocem: Tu quidem filius Excelsi eras, sed sicut homo morieris, et sicut unus de principibus cades (Psal. lxxxi, 6, 7). Quis non ab huius tonitrui voce formidet? O quam salubrius ad tactum angeli nervus femoris Iacob emarcuit (Gen. xxxii, 25), quam angeli superbientis intumuit, evanuit, ruit. Utinam et meum nervum angelus tangat ut marcescat, si forte ex hac infirmitate incipiam proficere, qui ex mea firmitate non possum nisi deficere. Lego profecto: Quod infirmum est Dei, fortius est hominibus (I Cor. i, 25). Sic quoque Apostolus de suo nervo conquestus, quem angelus non Domini, sed Satanae colaphizabat, responsum audivit: Sufficit tibi gratia mea; nam virtus in infirmitate perficitur. Quae virtus? Ipse Apostolus respondeat: Libenter gloriabor in infirmitatibus meis, ut inhabitet in me virtus Christi (II Cor. xii, 9). Sed nondum forsitan intelligis, de qua specialiter dixerit, quia Christus omnes virtutes habuit. Sed, cum omnes habuerit, prae omnibus tamen unam, id est humilitatem, nobis in se commendavit, cum ait: Discite a me, quia mitis sum et humilis corde (Matth. xi, 29).
segments.en: So much for the proud. But what of their head? what of him who is called king over all the children of pride (Job 41:25)? He, it is said, stood not in the truth (John 8:44): and elsewhere, I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven (Luke 10:18). Why this, if not because of pride? Woe to me if he who knows high things from afar should see me also growing proud, and should thunder against me that terrible voice: You were indeed a son of the Most High, but you shall die like a man, and fall like one of the princes (Ps. 81:6–7). Who would not fear before this voice of thunder? O how much more healthful that the sinew of Jacob’s thigh shrank at the angel’s touch (Gen. 32:25), than that it should swell, vanish, and fall at the touch of the angel of pride. Would that an angel would touch my sinew too, that it may shrink, if perhaps from this weakness I may begin to make progress, I who from my own strength can only fail. I read indeed: What is weak in God is stronger than men (1 Cor. 1:25). So also the Apostle, complaining of his own sinew, which an angel not of the Lord but of Satan was buffeting, heard the reply: My grace is sufficient for you; for virtue is made perfect in weakness. What virtue? Let the Apostle himself answer: Gladly will I glory in my weaknesses, that the virtue of Christ may dwell in me (2 Cor. 12:9). But perhaps you do not yet understand of which he spoke in particular, because Christ had all the virtues. Yet though he had them all, he commended to us in himself above all one, that is humility, when he said: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart (Matt. 11:29).

segments.la: Libenter igitur et ego, Domine Iesu, gloriabor, si potero, in mea infirmitate, in mei nervi contractione, ut tua virtus, id est humilitas, perficiatur in me. Nam sufficit mihi gratia tua, cum defecerit virtus mea. Pedem profecto gratiae fortiter figens, et meum qui infirmus est, leniter trahens, securus ascendam per scalam humilitatis, donec veritati adhaerens, ad latitudinem transeam charitatis. Tunc psallam cum gratiarum actione, et dicam: Statuisti in loco spatioso pedes meos (Psal. xxx, 9). Sic arcta via cautius strictim inceditur, sic ardua scala tutius pedetentim ascenditur; sic miro modo licet pigrius, ad veritatem tamen firmius claudicando ascenditur. Sed, heu mihi, quia incolatus meus prolongatus est (Psal. cxix, 5)! Quis dabit mihi pennas sicut columbae, quibus celerius volem ad veritatem, ut iam requiescam in charitate (Psal. liv, 7)? Quae quoniam desunt, deduc me, Domine, in via tua, et ingrediar in veritate tua, et veritas liberabit me. Vae mihi quod de illa descendi. Nisi enim prius leviter, inaniter descendissem, in ascendendo tamdiu, tam graviter non laborassem. Sed quid dico, Descendi? nam fortasse rectius Cecidi dixerim. Nisi quia forte sicut nemo repente fit summus, sed gradatim quisque ascendit: sic nemo repente fit pessimus, sed paulatim descendit. Alioquin quomodo stabit illud: Impius cunctis diebus vitae suae superbit (Iob xv, 20)? Denique sunt viae, quae videntur hominibus bonae, et tamen ad malum deducunt.
segments.en: Gladly therefore will I too, Lord Jesus, glory, if I can, in my weakness, in the shrinking of my sinew, that your virtue, that is humility, may be made perfect in me. For your grace is sufficient for me, when my strength has failed. Setting the foot of grace firmly, and drawing mine, which is weak, gently after, I will climb in safety by the ladder of humility, until, clinging to the truth, I pass over to the breadth of charity. Then I will sing with thanksgiving, and say: You have set my feet in a spacious place (Ps. 30:9). So the narrow way is walked more cautiously, close; so the steep ladder is climbed more safely, step by step; so, by a wondrous way, though more slowly, one climbs more firmly to the truth by limping. But woe is me, that my sojourn is prolonged (Ps. 119:5)! Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly more quickly to the truth, and already rest in charity (Ps. 54:7)? Since these are wanting, lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth, and the truth will set me free. Woe to me that I came down from it. For if I had not first come down lightly, emptily, I should not have labored so long, so heavily, in going up. But why do I say, I came down? perhaps I should more rightly say, I fell. Unless perhaps because, just as no one becomes highest all at once, but each climbs little by little: so no one becomes worst all at once, but goes down little by little. Otherwise how will that stand: The wicked man is proud all the days of his life (Job 15:20)? Finally there are ways that seem good to men, and yet lead to evil.

segments.la: Est ergo via descensionis, sicut et ascensionis. Et via est ad bonum, et via est ad malum. Cave malam, elige bonam. Si per te non potes, ora cum propheta, et dic: Viam iniquitatis amove a me. Quomodo? Et de lege tua miserere mei (Psal. cxviii, 29). Illa scilicet lege, quam dedisti delinquentibus in via, id est derelinquentibus veritatem, de quibus unus ego sum, qui vere a veritate cecidi. Sed numquid qui cadit, non adiiciet ut resurgat? Propter hoc viam veritatis elegi, qua ascendam humiliatus, unde superbiendo descendi. Ascendam, inquam, et psallam: Bonum mihi, Domine, quod humiliasti me; bonum mihi lex oris tui super millia auri et argenti (Psal. cxviii, 71, 72). Duas tibi vias videtur David proposuisse, sed unam noveris esse; ipsam tamen a se diversam, et diversis nominibus appellatam, aut iniquitatis propter descendentes, aut veritatis propter ascendentes: quia et iidem gradus sunt ascendentium in solium, et descendentium; et eadem via accedentium ad civitatem, et recedentium; et unum ostium est ingredientium domum, et egredientium. Per unam denique scalam ascendentes Angeli, et descendentes Iacob apparuerunt (Gen. xxviii, 12). Quo spectant haec? Ut videlicet si ad veritatem redire cupis, non necesse sit tibi quaerere novam quam non nosti, sed notam qua descendisti: quatenus reciprocis gressibus tua ipse vestigia sequens, per eosdem gradus humiliatus ascendas, per quos superbiendo descenderas: ita ut qui duodecimus superbiae fuit descendenti, primus humilitatis sit ascendenti; undecimus, inveniatur secundus; decimus, tertius; nonus, quartus; octavus, quintus; septimus, sextus; sextus, septimus; quintus, octavus; quartus, nonus; tertius, decimus; secundus, undecimus; primus, duodecimus. Quibus superbiae gradibus in te inventis, immo recognitis, iam non laboras in quaerendo viam humilitatis.
segments.en: There is then a way of descent, as there is of ascent. There is a way to good, and a way to evil. Beware the evil, choose the good. If you cannot of yourself, pray with the prophet, and say: Remove from me the way of iniquity. How? And out of your law have mercy on me (Ps. 118:29). That law, namely, which you gave to those who went astray in the way, that is, who forsook the truth, of whom I am one, who have indeed fallen from the truth. But does he who falls not add that he may rise again? For this reason I have chosen the way of truth, that, humbled, I may climb from where I came down by pride. I will go up, I say, and I will sing: It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me; the law of your mouth is good to me above thousands of gold and silver (Ps. 118:71–72). David may seem to have set two ways before you, but you should know they are one; the same, yet different from itself, and called by different names: of iniquity for those going down, of truth for those going up. For the same steps serve those climbing a throne and those coming down; the same road those approaching a city and those withdrawing; and there is one door for those entering a house and those going out. On one ladder, finally, the angels appeared to Jacob going up and going down (Gen. 28:12). What do these things look to? Namely, that if you desire to return to the truth, you need not seek a new way you do not know, but the known way by which you came down: so that, following your own footprints with returning steps, you may climb, humbled, by the same degrees by which you had come down in pride—so that what was twelfth of pride for the one going down is first of humility for the one going up; the eleventh is found second; the tenth, third; the ninth, fourth; the eighth, fifth; the seventh, sixth; the sixth, seventh; the fifth, eighth; the fourth, ninth; the third, tenth; the second, eleventh; the first, twelfth. When you have found these steps of pride in yourself—or rather recognized them—you no longer labor in searching for the way of humility.

title.la: Altera pars tractatus: De duodecim gradibus superbiae
title.en: Part II: The twelve steps of pride

title.la: De primo superbiae gradu, qui est curiositas
title.en: The first step of pride, which is curiosity

segments.la: Primus itaque superbiae gradus est curiositas. Hanc autem talibus indiciis deprehendes. Si videris monachum, de quo prius bene confidebas, ubicumque stat, ambulat, sedet, oculis incipientem vagari, caput erectum, aures portare suspensas: e motibus exterioris hominis interiorem immutatum agnoscas. Vir quippe vaferosus oculorum nutu facile deprehenditur (Prov. vi, 12–13): et ex insolenti corporis motu recens animi morbus deprehenditur; qui dum a sui circumspectione torpescit incuria sui, curiosam in alios festinat. Qui enim seipsum ignorat, foras mittitur, ut haedos pascat (Cantic. i, 7). Haedos quippe, qui peccatum significant, recte oculos auresque appellaverim: quoniam sicut mors per peccatum in orbem, sic per has fenestras intrat ad mentem. In his ergo pascendis se occupat curiosus, dum scire non curat qualem se reliquerit intus. Et vere si te vigilanter, homo, attendis, mirum est si ad aliud unquam intendas. Audi, curiose, Salomonem; audi, stulte, Sapientem. Omni custodia, inquit, custodi cor tuum (Prov. iv, 23): ut omnes videlicet sensus tui vigilent ad id, unde vita procedit, custodiendum. Quo enim a te, o curiose, recedis? Cui te interim committis? Ut quid audes oculos levare ad caelum, qui peccasti in caelum? Terram intuere, ut cognoscas teipsum. Ipsa te tibi repraesentabit, quia terra es, et in terram ibis.
segments.en: The first step of pride, then, is curiosity. You will detect it by such signs as these. If you see a monk, of whom you used to think well, wherever he stands, walks, or sits, beginning to wander with his eyes, head up, ears cocked: from the motions of the outer man recognize that the inner has been changed. The crafty man is easily caught by the wink of the eyes (Prov. 6:12–13); and from the insolent motion of the body a fresh disease of the soul is detected. While it grows numb in watching over itself, by carelessness of itself it hurries, curious, toward others. He who does not know himself is sent outside to feed the kids (Song 1:7). The kids, which signify sin, I would rightly call the eyes and the ears: for as death comes into the world through sin, so through these windows it enters the mind. The curious man occupies himself in feeding them, while he does not care to know what he has left inside himself. And truly, if you attend to yourself watchfully, O man, it is a wonder if you ever attend to anything else. Hear, curious one, Solomon; hear, fool, the Wise. With all watchfulness, he says, keep your heart (Prov. 4:23): that all your senses may watch to guard that from which life proceeds. For where, O curious man, do you withdraw from yourself? To whom do you meanwhile commit yourself? Why do you dare to lift your eyes to heaven, you who have sinned against heaven? Look at the earth, that you may know yourself. It will show you to yourself, for you are earth, and to earth you will go.

segments.la: Duabus tamen ex causis inculpabiliter oculos levas, ut vel petas auxilium, vel impendas. Levavit oculos David in montes, ut peteret (Psal. cxx, 1): levavit et Dominus super turbas, ut impenderet (Ioan. vi, 5). Alter miserabiliter, alter misericorditer, ambo inculpabiliter. Tu quoque si locum, tempus et causam considerans, tua vel fratris necessitate oculos levas: non solum non culpo, sed et plurimum laudo. Hoc enim excusat miseria, illud commendat misericordia. Sin alias, non Prophetae, non Domini, sed Dinae aut Evae, imo ipsius Satanae imitatorem te dixerim. Dina namque, dum ad pascendos haedos egreditur, ipsa patri, et sua sibi virginitas rapitur (Gen. xxxiv, 1–2). O Dina, quid necesse est ut videas mulieres alienigenas? Qua necessitate? aut qua utilitate? An sola curiositate? Etsi tu otiose vides, sed non otiose videris. Tu curiose spectas, sed curiosius spectaris. Quis crederet tunc illam tuam curiosam otiositatem, vel otiosam curiositatem, fore post sic non otiosam, sed tibi, tuis, hostibusque tam perniciosam?
segments.en: There are two reasons, even so, for which you may raise your eyes without blame: to ask help, or to give it. David lifted his eyes to the hills, to ask (Ps. 120:1); the Lord lifted his over the crowds, to give (John 6:5). One miserably, the other mercifully; both without blame. And you too, if considering place, time, and cause you lift your eyes in your own or a brother’s need, I do not blame you: I praise you much. Misery excuses the one; mercy commends the other. Otherwise I should call you an imitator not of the Prophet, not of the Lord, but of Dinah or of Eve, even of Satan himself. For Dinah, when she went out to feed the kids, was herself snatched from her father, and her virginity from her (Gen. 34:1–2). O Dinah, what need was there that you should see the foreign women? By what necessity? or what use? Or by curiosity alone? Even if you look idly, you are not idly looked at. You gaze curiously, but you are gazed at more curiously. Who would have believed then that that curious idleness, or idle curiosity, of yours would afterward prove not idle, but so ruinous to you, to yours, and to your enemies?

segments.la: Tu quoque, o Eva, in paradiso posita es, ut cum viro tuo opereris et custodias illum: si iniunctum perfeceris, quandoque transitura ad melius, ubi nec opus sit te in aliquo opere occupari, nec de custodia sollicitari. Omne lignum paradisi tibi conceditur ad vescendum, praeter illud, quod dicitur, scientiae boni et mali (Gen. ii, 16–17). Si enim caetera bona sunt, et sapiunt bonum, quid est opus edere de ligno, quod sapit etiam malum? Non plus sapere, quam oportet sapere (Rom. xii, 3). Sapere enim malum, sapere non est, sed desipere. Serva ergo commissum, exspecta promissum; cave prohibitum, ne perdas concessum. Quid tuam mortem tam intente intueris? Quid illo tam crebro vagantia lumina iacis? Quid spectare libet, quod manducare non licet? Oculos, inquis, tendo, non manum. Non est interdictum ne videam, sed ne comedam. An non licet oculos quo volo levare, quos Deus in mea posuit potestate? Ad quod Apostolus: Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia expediunt (I Cor. vi, 12). Etsi culpa non est, culpae tamen indicium est. Nisi enim mens minus se curiose servaret, tua curiositas tempus vacuum non haberet. Etsi culpa non est, culpae tamen occasio est, et indicium commissae, et causa est committendae. Te enim intenta ad aliud, latenter interim in cor tuum serpens illabitur, blande alloquitur. Blanditiis rationem, mendaciis timorem compescit. Nequaquam, inquiens, morieris (Gen. iii, 4). Auget curam, dum incitat gulam; acuit curiositatem, dum suggerit cupiditatem. Offert tandem prohibitum, et aufert concessum: porrigit pomum, et subripit paradisum. Hauris virus peritura, et perituros paritura. Perit salus, non destitit partus. Nascimur, morimur: ideoque nascimur morituri, quia prius morimur nascituri. Propterea grave iugum super omnes filios tuos usque in hodiernum diem.
segments.en: And you, O Eve, were placed in paradise to work with your husband and to keep it: if you had finished what was enjoined, you would at some time have passed to something better, where there would be no need for you to be occupied in any work, or anxious about keeping. Every tree of paradise is granted you for food, except that which is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:16–17). For if the rest are good, and taste of good, what need is there to eat of a tree that tastes of evil too? Not to be wise above what it is fitting to be wise (Rom. 12:3). For to taste evil is not to be wise, but to be unwise. Keep then what is committed, wait for what is promised; beware what is forbidden, lest you lose what is granted. Why do you look so intently at your own death? Why do you so often cast wandering lights that way? Why does it please you to look at what it is not lawful to eat? “I stretch my eyes,” you say, “not my hand. It is not forbidden that I should see, but that I should eat. May I not lift my eyes where I will, which God has placed in my power?” To which the Apostle: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient (1 Cor. 6:12). Even if it is not a fault, it is still a sign of a fault. For if the mind were not keeping itself too little curiously, your curiosity would have no empty time. Even if it is not a fault, it is still an occasion of a fault, and a sign of one committed, and a cause of one to be committed. For while you are intent on something else, the serpent meanwhile glides secretly into your heart and speaks softly. By blandishments he weakens reason, by lies he checks fear. You shall not die, he says (Gen. 3:4). He increases care while he inflames the gullet; he sharpens curiosity while he suggests desire. At last he offers what is forbidden and takes away what is granted: he holds out the apple and steals paradise. You drink the poison, about to perish, and about to bring forth those who will perish. Salvation perishes; childbearing does not cease. We are born, we die: and therefore we are born to die, because we first die in order to be born. Therefore a heavy yoke is upon all your sons even to this day.

segments.la: Sed et tu, signaculum similitudinis, non in paradiso, sed in deliciis paradisi Dei positus es (Ezech. xxviii, 12–13). Quid amplius quaerere debes? Plenus ergo sapientia, et perfectus decore, altiora te ne quaesieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris. Sta in te, ne cadas a te, si ambulas in magnis et in mirabilibus super te. Sed quid interim ex obliquo intendis ad aquilonem? Iam te video, iam te perspicio nescio quae supra te curiosius alta rimantem. Ponam, inquis, sedem meam ad aquilonem (Isa. xiv, 13). Caeteris astantibus caelicolis, dum tu solus sedere affectas, fratrum concordiam, totius caelestis patriae pacem, ipsius, quantum in te est, quietem Trinitatis infestas. Quo te tua, miser, curiositas ducit, ut praesumptione singulari non dubites civibus scandalum, iniuriam facere Regi? Millia millium ministrant ei, et decies centena millia assistunt ei (Dan. vii, 10), ubi nemo sedere perhibetur, nisi solus is qui sedet super Cherubim, cui a caeteris ministratur: et tu nescio quae prae caeteris perspiciendo differentius, curiosius inquirendo, irreverentius pervadendo, sedem tibi collocas in caelo, ut sis similis Altissimo? Quo fine? qua fiducia? Metire, insipiens, vires, pensa finem, excogita modum. Sciente hoc Altissimo praesumis, an nesciente? volente, an non volente? Sed quomodo malum quodcumque machinaris, aut velle, aut ignorare potest, cuius optima voluntas, cuius perfecta scientia est? Numquid autem et scire, et nolle non dubitas, sed non posse resistere putas? At vero nisi te conditum esse dubitaveris, dubitare te non crediderim de omnipotentia, sive de omnimoda scientia ac bonitate Conditoris, qui te de nihilo potuit, talem scivit, tantum condere voluit. Quomodo ergo Deum consentire aestimas, quod fieri nolit, ac refellere possit? An forte in te video compleri, imo a te initiari, quod post te, et per te a tui similibus in terris frequentatum solet vulgariter dici: Privatus dominus temerarios nutrit? An oculus tuus nequam est, quia ille bonus? De cuius bonitate dum fiduciam nefariam sumis, factus es et contra scientiam impudens, et contra potentiam audax.
segments.en: And you too, seal of likeness, were placed not in paradise but in the delights of the paradise of God (Ezek. 28:12–13). What more should you seek? You are full of wisdom, then, and perfect in beauty; do not seek things too high for you, and do not search out things too strong for you. Stand in yourself, lest you fall from yourself, if you walk in things great and wonderful above you. But why in the meantime do you glance aslant toward the north? Already I see you, already I perceive you peering too curiously into I know not what heights above you. I will set my seat in the north, you say (Isa. 14:13). While the other heavenly citizens stand, you alone desire to sit, and so far as in you lies you trouble the brethren’s concord, the peace of the whole heavenly homeland, the rest of the Trinity itself. Where does your wretched curiosity lead you, that with singular presumption you do not hesitate to scandalize the citizens and do injury to the King? Thousands of thousands minister to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him (Dan. 7:10), where no one is said to sit except he alone who sits upon the Cherubim, whom the rest serve: and you, I know not what, looking out more distinctly than the rest, inquiring more curiously, invading more irreverently, set yourself a seat in heaven, that you may be like the Most High? With what end? with what confidence? Measure your strength, you fool; weigh the end; think out the means. Do you presume this with the Most High knowing, or not knowing? willing, or not willing? But how can he whose will is best, whose knowledge is perfect, either will or be ignorant of whatever evil you contrive? Or do you not doubt that he knows and is unwilling, but think he cannot resist? Yet unless you have doubted that you were created, I would not believe you could doubt the omnipotence, or the complete knowledge and goodness, of the Creator, who could make you from nothing, knew you such, and willed to make you so great. How then do you suppose God consents to what he does not wish to be done, and can prevent? Do I perhaps see fulfilled in you—no, begun from you—what after you, and through you, is commonly said among those like you on earth: A private master feeds reckless men? Is your eye evil because he is good? And while you take a wicked confidence from his goodness, you have become shameless against his knowledge, and bold against his power.

segments.la: Hoc est enim, o impie, hoc est quod cogitas; haec est iniquitas, quam meditaris in cubili tuo, et dicis: Putas Creator opus suum destruat? Scio quidem quia non latet Deum qualiscumque cogitatio mea: Deus enim est. Nec placet ei talis cogitatio mea, quia bonus est. Sed nec si velit, ego effugiam manus eius, quia potens est. Numquid tamen mihi timendum est? Si enim cum bonus sit, non potest illi placere malum meum, quanto minus suum? Meum quippe dixerim contra eius voluntatem aliquid velle; suum autem, si vindicet sese. Tam ergo quodcumque scelus non valet velle ulcisci, quam nec vult, nec valet sua bonitate privari. Fallis te, miser, fallis te, non Deum. Te, inquam, fallis, et mentitur iniquitas sibi, non Deo. Dolose quidem agis, sed in conspectu eius. Te ergo fallis, non Deum. Et quia de magno eius bono in te, tu magnum in eum excogitas malum, merito iniquitas tua invenitur ad odium. Quae maior namque iniquitas, quam ut inde a te Creator contemnatur, unde plus amari merebatur? Quae maior iniquitas, quam cum de potentia Dei non dubites, quin te scilicet destruere possit qui condere potuit; confisus tamen de multa eius dulcedine, qua speras eum nolle vindicare cum possit; mala pro bonis, odium pro dilectione retribuas?
segments.en: For this, O unholy one, this is what you think; this is the iniquity you meditate on your bed, and you say: Do you think the Creator will destroy his own work? I know that no thought of mine, of whatever kind, is hidden from God: for he is God. Nor does such a thought of mine please him, because he is good. Nor, if he should will it, shall I escape his hand, because he is mighty. Yet is it to be feared by me? For if, being good, he cannot be pleased by my evil, how much less by his own? Mine, I should call it, to will something against his will; his, if he avenge himself. Therefore he cannot will to punish any crime, any more than he wills or is able to be deprived of his own goodness. You deceive yourself, wretch; you deceive yourself, not God. Yourself, I say, you deceive, and iniquity lies to itself, not to God. You act deceitfully, but in his sight. Therefore you deceive yourself, not God. And because from his great goodness toward you, you contrive great evil against him, your iniquity is found to be hatred. For what greater iniquity than that the Creator should be scorned by you for the very thing by which he most deserved to be loved? What greater iniquity than that, while you do not doubt God’s power—that he who could create you can destroy you—yet trusting in his great sweetness, by which you hope he will be unwilling to avenge though he can, you repay evils for goods, hatred for love?

segments.la: Haec, inquam, iniquitas, non ira momentanea, sed odio digna est sempiterno, qua tuo dulcissimo et altissimo Domino, licet invito, desideras tamen ac speras aequari, quatenus semper videat quod doleat, dum te socium habeat cum nolit, nec deiciat cum possit; quin potius eligat ipse dolere, quam te patiatur perire; possit quidem deicere si velit, sed prae dulcedine, ut aestimas, velle non possit. Certe si talis est qualem putas, tanto nequius agis, si non amas. Et si ille patitur aliquid fieri contra se potius, quam ipse aliquid faciat contra te; quanta malitia est, ut vel tu non parcas illi, qui sibi non parcit, parcendo tibi? Absit tamen ab eius perfectione, ut quia dulcis est, iustus non sit, quasi simul dulcis et iustus esse non possit: cum melior sit iusta dulcedo, quam remissa; imo virtus non sit dulcedo sine iustitia. Quia igitur gratuitae Dei bonitati, qua gratis factus es, ingratus existis, iustitiam vero quam expertus non es, non metuis; ideoque audacter committis culpam, de qua falso tibi promittis impunitatem: iam ecce iustum senties, quem bonum nosti, cadens in foveam, quam paras auctori: ut dum scilicet talem in eum poenam machinaris, qua tamen valeat carere si velit, sed ut putas non valeat velle: et ideo nec carere ea utique bonitate, qua neminem expertus es illum punisse: talem iustus Deus iustissime in te retorqueat poenam, qui nec valet, nec debet pati suam impune bonitatem offendi: sic utique temperans in vindicta sententiam, ut, si velis resipiscere, non neget veniam; secundum tamen duritiam tuam et cor impaenitens, non possis velle, et ideo nec poena carere.
segments.en: This iniquity, I say, is worthy not of a moment’s anger but of everlasting hatred: by it you desire and hope to be made equal to your most sweet and most high Lord, though he is unwilling, so that he may always see what grieves him, while he has you as a companion when he does not wish it, and does not cast you down when he can; rather he would choose to suffer himself than let you perish. He could cast you down if he willed, but because of his sweetness, as you suppose, he cannot will it. Surely if he is such as you think, you act so much the more wickedly if you do not love him. And if he suffers something to be done against himself rather than do something against you, what malice it is that you should not spare him who does not spare himself in sparing you? Yet far be it from his perfection that, because he is sweet, he should not be just, as if he could not be sweet and just at once: since a just sweetness is better than a slack one; indeed sweetness without justice is not a virtue. Because therefore you are ungrateful for the gratuitous goodness of God, by which you were made freely, and you do not fear the justice you have not experienced, you therefore boldly commit a fault from which you falsely promise yourself impunity: now you will find him just whom you have known as good, falling into the pit you prepare for your Maker. For while you contrive against him a punishment which he can still avoid if he wills, but, as you think, cannot will to avoid, and therefore cannot be without that goodness by which you have never known him to punish anyone: let the just God most justly turn such a punishment back on you, who neither can nor ought to suffer his goodness to be offended with impunity; so moderating the sentence in vengeance that, if you should will to come to your senses, he would not refuse pardon; yet according to your hardness and impenitent heart you cannot will it, and therefore cannot be without the punishment.

segments.la: Sed iam audi calumniam: Caelum, inquit, mihi sedes est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum (Isa. lxvi, 1). Non dixit, Oriens, aut Occidens, aut una aliqua caeli plaga: sed, Totum caelum mihi sedes est. Non potes ergo in parte sedere caeli, cum ille totum elegerit sibi. In terra non potes, quia scabellum pedum eius est. Terra etenim locus solidus est, ubi sedet Ecclesia, fundata supra firmam petram. Quid facies? E caelo pulsus, in terra remanere non potes. Elige ergo tibi in aere locum, non ad sedendum, sed ad volandum: ut qui tentasti concutere statum aeternitatis, poenam sentias propriae fluctuationis. Te ergo fluctuante inter caelum et terram, sedet Dominus super solium excelsum et elevatum, et plena est omnis terra maiestate eius (Isa. vi, 1–3), ut nusquam nisi in aere invenias locum.
segments.en: But now hear the charge: Heaven, he says, is my seat, and the earth the footstool of my feet (Isa. 66:1). He did not say East, or West, or some one region of heaven: but, The whole heaven is my seat. You cannot therefore sit in a part of heaven, since he has chosen the whole for himself. On earth you cannot, because it is the footstool of his feet. For the earth is a solid place, where the Church sits, founded upon a firm rock. What will you do? Driven from heaven, you cannot remain on earth. Choose then a place for yourself in the air, not for sitting but for flying: that you who tried to shake the standing of eternity may feel the punishment of your own fluctuation. So while you toss between heaven and earth, the Lord sits upon a throne high and lifted up, and the whole earth is full of his majesty (Isa. 6:1–3), so that you may find a place nowhere except in the air.

segments.la: Seraphim namque aliis quidem alis suae contemplationis de throno ad scabellum, de scabello ad thronum volantia, aliis caput Domini pedesque velantia, ad hoc ibi posita puto, ut sicut homini peccanti paradisi per Cherubim prohibetur ingressus, ita et per Seraphim tuae curiositati modus imponatur: quatenus nec caeli iam magis impudenter quam prudenter arcana rimeris, nec Ecclesiae mysteria cognoscas in terris; sed solis contentus sis cordibus superborum, qui nec in terra dignantur esse sicut caeteri hominum, nec sicut Angeli volant ad caelum. Licet vero et caput in caelo, et pedes in terra a te abscondantur, quiddam tamen tibi medium videndum ad invidendum dumtaxat permittitur: dum suspensus in aere, descendentes quidem per te et ascendentes Angelos intueris; sed quid vel audiant in caelis, vel nuntient terris, penitus nescis.
segments.en: For the Seraphim, flying with some wings of their contemplation from the throne to the footstool and from the footstool to the throne, and with others covering the Lord’s head and feet, are placed there, I think, for this: that as by the Cherubim entrance to paradise is forbidden to sinful man, so by the Seraphim a limit may be set to your curiosity: so that you may no longer, more shamelessly than prudently, search out the secrets of heaven, nor know the mysteries of the Church on earth, but be content with the hearts of the proud alone, who do not deign to be on earth like the rest of men, nor fly to heaven like the Angels. Yet although both the head in heaven and the feet on earth are hidden from you, some middle thing is still permitted you to see, if only to envy: while, hung in the air, you watch the Angels descending past you and ascending; but what they hear in heaven, or announce on earth, you do not know at all.

segments.la: O Lucifer, qui mane oriebaris, imo non iam lucifer, sed noctifer, aut etiam mortifer, rectus cursus tuus erat ab oriente ad meridiem, et tu praepostero ordine tendis ad aquilonem? Quanto magis ad alta festinas, tanto celerius ad occasum declinas. Velim tamen curiosius, o curiose, intentionem tuae curiositatis inquirere. Ponam, inquis, sedem meam ad aquilonem (Isa. xiv, 13). Nec aquilonem hunc corporalem, nec sedem hanc (cum sis spiritus) intelligo materialem. Puto autem per aquilonem, reprobandos homines fuisse designatos: per sedem, potestatem in illos. Quos utique in praescientia Dei, quanto ei vicinior, tanto caeteris perspicacior praevidens, nullo quidem sapientiae radio coruscantes, nullo spiritus amore ferventes, velut vacuum repereris locum, affectasti super illos dominium, quos quadam tuae astutiae claritate perfunderes, tuae malitiae aestibus inflammares: ut quomodo Altissimus sua sapientia ac bonitate omnibus filiis obedientiae praeerat, ita et tu super omnes filios superbiae rex constitutus, tua eos astuta malitia, ac malitiosa astutia regeres, per quod Altissimo similis esses. Sed miror cum in praescientia Dei tuum praevideris principatum, cur non eadem praevidisti et praecipitium? Nam si praevidisti, quae insania fuit, ut cum tanta miseria cuperes principari, ut malles misere praeesse, quam feliciter subesse? An non expediebat participem esse plagarum illarum luminosarum, quam principem tenebrarum harum? Sed credibilius est, quod non praevidisti: aut propter illam causam, quam superius dixi, quia Dei bonitatem attendens, dixisti in corde tuo, Non requiret (Psal. x, 13), propter quod, o impie, Deum irritasti; aut quia viso principatu, statim in oculo superbiae trabes excrevit, qua interposita casum videre non potuisti.
segments.en: O Lucifer, who rose in the morning—no longer light-bearer, but night-bearer, or even death-bearer—your right course was from the east to the south, and do you by a reversed order tend toward the north? The more you hurry to the heights, the more swiftly you decline to your setting. Yet I would still inquire more curiously, O curious one, into the intention of your curiosity. I will set my seat in the north, you say (Isa. 14:13). I do not take this north as bodily, nor this seat (since you are a spirit) as material. I think by the north were meant men to be reprobated; by the seat, power over them. These, in the foreknowledge of God, seeing more clearly than the rest as you were nearer to him, shining with no ray of wisdom, burning with no love of the spirit, you found as it were an empty place, and you claimed dominion over them, that you might pour into them a certain brightness of your cunning, and inflame them with the heats of your malice: so that as the Most High by his wisdom and goodness ruled all the sons of obedience, you too, made king over all the sons of pride, might rule them by your cunning malice and malicious cunning, and by that be like the Most High. But I wonder, when in God’s foreknowledge you foresaw your principality, why you did not by the same foresight foresee the precipice also. For if you did foresee it, what madness was it that you should desire to rule with such misery, that you would rather be wretchedly over others than happily under them? Was it not better to be a partner of those regions of light than prince of these of darkness? But it is more credible that you did not foresee it: either for that cause I gave above, because attending to God’s goodness you said in your heart, He will not require it (Ps. 10:13), and for that, O unholy one, you provoked God; or because, when the principality was seen, the beam of pride at once grew in the eye, and with that interposed you could not see the fall.

segments.la: Sic Ioseph cum praevidisset exaltationem suam (Gen. xxxvii, 7–9), non tamen praescivit sui venditionem, quamvis propior esset venditio, quam exaltatio. Non quod tantum patriarcham in superbiam crediderim incidisse: sed ut eius exemplo pateat, quod hi qui futura praevident per spiritum prophetiae, etsi non omnia, non ideo tamen putandi sunt nulla praevidisse. Quod si quis contendat in eo quod somnia sua adhuc adolescentulus narrabat, quorum tunc mysterium ignorabat, vanitatem posse notari; ego tamen mysterio magis sive simplicitati pueri deputandum arbitror, quam vanitati. Quae tamen, si qua fuit, per ea quae passus legitur, potuit expiari. Nonnullis enim aliqua aliquando de se per revelationem iucunda monstrantur, quae etsi humanus animus absque ulla vanitate scire non potest, non minus ideo eveniet quod monstratum est; sic tamen ut illa vanitas impunita non sit, qua de magnitudine revelationis aut promissionis in se vel leviter exsultavit. Sicut enim medicus, non solum unguento, sed igne utitur et ferro, quo omne quod in vulnere sanando superfluum excreverit, secet et urat, ne sanitatem, quae ex unguento procedit, impediat: sic medicus animarum Deus huiusmodi animae procurat tentationes, immittit tribulationes, quibus afflicta et humiliata, gaudium vertat in luctum, revelationem putet illusionem. Unde fit ut vanitate careat, et veritas revelationis non pereat. Sic Pauli extollentia per stimulos carnis reprimitur (II Cor. xii, 7), et ipse revelationibus crebris attollitur. Sic Zachariae infidelitas linguae obligatione mulctatur (Luc. i, 20), et angeli veritas suo in tempore manifestanda non mutatur. Sic, sic per gloriam et ignobilitatem sancti proficiunt, dum inter singularia dona quae recipiunt, communi hominum vanitate aliquid cernunt, non obliviscantur quod sunt.
segments.en: So Joseph, when he had foreseen his exaltation (Gen. 37:7–9), did not yet foresee his being sold, although the sale was nearer than the exaltation. Not that I would believe so great a patriarch had fallen into pride: but that by his example it may be clear that those who foresee future things by the spirit of prophecy, though they do not foresee all, are not therefore to be thought to have foreseen nothing. If anyone contends that vanity can be noted in this, that as a youth he still told his dreams, whose mystery he then did not know, I still think it should be put down rather to the mystery or to the boy’s simplicity than to vanity. And if there was any, it could be atoned for by the things he is read to have suffered. For to some, pleasant things about themselves are sometimes shown by revelation, which, even if the human mind cannot know them without some vanity, what was shown will nonetheless come to pass; yet so that that vanity is not unpunished, by which it lightly exulted in itself at the greatness of the revelation or the promise. For as a physician uses not only ointment but fire and iron, to cut and burn away whatever has grown superfluous in the wound that is to be healed, lest it hinder the health that comes from the ointment: so God, the physician of souls, procures temptations for a soul of this kind, sends tribulations, by which, afflicted and humbled, it may turn joy into mourning and think the revelation an illusion. Hence it comes that it is without vanity, and the truth of the revelation does not perish. So Paul’s being lifted up is checked by the goads of the flesh (2 Cor. 12:7), and he himself is lifted by frequent revelations. So Zechariah’s unbelief is punished by the binding of his tongue (Luke 1:20), and the angel’s truth, to be made manifest in its time, is not changed. So, so the saints advance by glory and ignominy, while among the singular gifts they receive they still discern something of the vanity common to men, and do not forget what they are.

segments.la: Sed, quid de revelationibus ad curiositatem? De quibus ut haec per excessum intermiscerem, inde occasio sumpta est, cum ostendere vellem, reprobum angelum ante casum suum sic potuisse praevidere illam, quam post accepit, in reprobos homines dominationem, ut tamen suam non praesciret damnationem. De quo etiam nonnullis quaestiunculis motis magis quam solutis, totius disputatiunculae haec summa sit: quod per curiositatem a veritate ceciderit, quia prius spectavit curiose, quod affectavit illicite, speravit praesumptuose. Iure igitur in gradibus superbiae primum curiositas vindicat sibi, quae etiam inventa est initium esse omnis peccati. Sed nisi haec citius cohibeatur, in levitatem animi, quae secundus gradus est, cito delabitur.
segments.en: But what of revelations for curiosity? The occasion of mixing these things in by a digression was taken from this, when I wished to show that the reprobate angel, before his fall, could so foresee that dominion over reprobate men which he afterward received, that he still did not foreknow his own damnation. About which, some little questions having been raised rather than solved, let this be the sum of the whole little dispute: that he fell from the truth by curiosity, because he first looked curiously at what he desired unlawfully and hoped for presumptuously. Rightly therefore among the steps of pride curiosity claims the first for itself, which has also been found to be the beginning of all sin. But unless this is more quickly restrained, it soon slips into levity of mind, which is the second step.

title.la: De secundo gradu superbiae qui est levitas animi
title.en: The second step of pride, which is levity of mind

segments.la: Monachus enim, qui sui negligens, alios curiose circumspicit, dum quosdam suspicit superiores: a quibusdam despicit inferiores: et in his quidem videt quod invidet, in illis quod irridet. Inde fit ut pro mobilitate oculorum levigatus animus, nulla utique sui cura aggravatus, motus per superbiam ad alta se erigat, modo per invidiam in ima demergatur: nunc per invidiam superior hebetescit, nunc per excellentiam pueriliter nitescit. In altero nequam, in altero vanus, utroque superbus existit: quia et quod invidet se dolet, et quod superat se gaudet, uter proprie excellentiae facit. Has autem animi vicissitudines nunc pauca et mordacia, nunc multa et inania: nunc risu, nunc luctu plena, semper vero irrationabilia indicant verba. Comparas, ais, hos duos primos superbiae gradus supremis duobus humilitatis: et vide si non in ultimo curiositas, in penultimo levitas cohibetur. Id ipsum in ceteris reperies, si alterutrum comparaveris. Sed iam ad tertium ducendo, nos descendendo veniamus.
segments.en: For the monk who, careless of himself, looks curiously at others, envies some as superiors and despises others as inferiors: in the one he sees what he envies, in the other what he mocks. So by the mobility of the eyes the mind is made light, not weighed down by any care of itself; now it lifts itself by pride to high things, now by envy it sinks to the depths. These turns of mind are shown by words now few and biting, now many and empty, now full of laughter, now of grief, but always unreasonable. Compare these first two steps of pride with the last two of humility, and see whether curiosity is not restrained in the last, levity in the last but one. You will find the same if you compare the rest. But now let us come, descending, to the third.

title.la: De tertio gradu superbiae qui est inepta laetitia
title.en: The third step of pride, which is unseasonable merriment

segments.la: Proprium est superborum, laeta semper appetere, et tristia devitare, iuxta illud: Cor stultorum ubi laetitia (Eccli. vii, 5). Unde et monachus, qui duos iam superbiae gradus descendit, dum per curiositatem ad animi levitatem devenit, cum gaudium quoque super appetit, frequenti videt interpolari tristitia, quam de bonis alterius concipit, impaciens sui, humilitatis, fugit ad consilium falsae consolationis. Hic illa moniche parte, qui sibi sua vilitas et aliena excellentia demonstratur, restringit curiositatem, ut totum se transferat in contrariam partem: quatenus in se quoque vilitatem non videat, in quo alter praecellit, semper dissimulet: ut dum devitat quod triste putatur, laetitia continuetur. Sicque fit ut quem sibi vicissim vindicabant gaudium et tristitia, solo possidere incipiat inepta laetitia. Hanc autem, in qua tertium tibi gradum constituo, accipe quibus eam signis vel in te deprehendas, vel in altero. Illum qui eiusmodi est, aut nunquam, aut raro gementem audies, aut lacrymantem videbis, Pulsa, si attendas, aut nisi otiosum, aut scurram volpes. In signis scurrilitas, in fronte hilaritas, vanitas in incessu. Pronus ad iocum, facilis ad rumptum in risu. Cunctis quippe quae in contemptibilia, et ideo tristia noverat, a memoria rasis; si quandoque, si cui iniuriam, admonitus, statim ante oculos mentis, dum nisi cogites nisi quod libet nec attendi si licet; iam risum tenet, iam ineptam laetitiam dissimulare non valet. Ut enim vesica collecto turgida vento punctoque forata exiguo, si stringitur, crepitat dum non possim effusus, sed strictim emissus aer: eodem quorundam sonitus reddit: sic monachus, ubi vanis scurrilibusque cor suum cogitationibus impleverit, propter disciplinam silentii non inveniens ventus vanitatis qua plenius egrediatur, inter angustias faucium per cachinnos excutitur. Saepe vultum pudibundus abscondit, claudit labia, dentes stringit; ridet non volens, cachinnat invitus. Cum que se pugans, instruxerit suis, per nares adhuc sorniatur.
segments.en: It belongs to the proud always to seek what is cheerful and to shun what is sad, according to that word: The heart of fools is where there is mirth (Sir. 7:5). This man, in whom I set the third step for you, you will hear groaning never or rarely, and seldom see weeping. If you attend, you will take him for an idle man or a buffoon. There is scurrility in his signs, cheerfulness on his brow, vanity in his gait. He is prone to a joke, easy to burst into laughter. As a bladder swollen with gathered wind, if pricked with a small hole and squeezed, crackles because the air cannot pour out at once but is let out in a thin stream: so the monk, when he has filled his heart with vain and scurrilous thoughts, and because of the discipline of silence cannot find a fuller way out for the wind of vanity, shakes it out in giggles between the narrows of the throat.

title.la: De quarto gradu superbiae, qui est iactantia
title.en: The fourth step of pride, which is boastfulness

segments.la: At postquam vanitas crescere, et vesica grossescere coeperit, necesse est ut in ampliori foramine, laxato sinu, ventositas eructetur, alioquin rumpetur. Sic monachus inepta redundante laetitia dum risu, vel signis eam aperire non sufficit, in Helione illud impleri: En venter meus, quasi mustum absque spiraculo, quod novas lagunculas disrumpit (Iob. xxxii, 19). Aut loquetur ergo, aut rumpetur. Ploeus est enim sermonibus, et coarctat eum spiritus uteri sui. Locum quaerit audiendi, causam nanciscitur loquendi. Interrogantem, non querenti respondet. Ipse quaerit, ipse solvit, et verba collocutoris imperfecta praevenit. Citi eum loquentis signo necesse est interrumpunt. Colloquium, quam longam, breve queritur intercallum; quantum putesit, ut ad fabulas revertatur post horam, non ut quoniam aedificet, sed ut scientiam iactet. Aedificare potest, sed non aedificare intendit. Non curat te docere, vel a te doceri ipse quod nescit: sed ut scire quis aestimet. Quod si de religione agitur, statim visiones et somnia proferuntur. Deinde laudat ieiunia, commendat vigilias, super omnia orationes exaltat de patientia, de humilitate, et de cunctis virtutibus plenissime, sed vanissime disputat. Et scilicet, ut diceris, dicas quod ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, et quia bonus homo de bono thesauro suo profert bona (Luc. vi, 45). Si ad ludicra sermo convertitur, in his quanto assuetior, tanto loquacior invenitur. Dicax, si audias rivum vanitatis, fluvium esse scurrilitatis es qui est. Non esse facilem aut promptum ad risum.
segments.en: But after vanity begins to grow and the bladder to swell, it must belch the wind through a wider opening, or it will burst. So the monk, when unseasonable merriment overflows and laughing or signs are not enough to let it out, has that of Elihu fulfilled in him: Behold my belly is as new wine without a vent, which bursts new bottles (Job 32:19). Either he will speak, or he will burst. He is full of words, and the spirit of his belly constrains him. He looks for a place to be heard, he finds a reason to talk. He answers one who does not ask. He himself questions, himself solves, and cuts off his partner’s unfinished words. If religion is the subject, visions and dreams are brought out at once. Then he praises fasts, commends vigils, exalts prayers above all; he discusses patience, humility, and all the virtues most fully, but most vainly. If the talk turns to light things, he is found more talkative the more he is used to them.

title.la: De quinto gradu superbiae, qui dicitur singularitas
title.en: The fifth step of pride, which is called singularity

segments.la: Turpe est ei, qui se supra ceteros iactat, si non plus ceteris aliquid agat, per quod ultra ceteros apparere. Proinde non sufficit ei quod communis monasterii regula, vel maiorum cohortantur exempla. Nec tamen melior esse studet, sed videri. Non melius vivere, sed videri vivere gestit, quatenus dicere possit: Non sum sicut ceteri hominum (Luc. xviii, 11). Plus sibi blanditur de uno ieiunio, quod ceteris prudentibus fecit, quam si cum ceteris septem viris ieiunavisset. Considerat sibi vicinus una oratiuncula peculiaris, quam tota psalmodia unius noctis. Inter prudentum crebro solet oculos iactare per mensas, ut si quem minus comedere viderit, vicem se doleat, et incipiat idipsum sibi crudelius subtrahere, quod necessarium victui infalegendum prudentum, plus gloriae metuentes detrimentum, quam famis cruciatum. Si quem macriorem, si quem pallidiorem perspexerit, vilem se aestimat, nunquam quiescit. Se quotidie aliquem sibi novum videre non potest, qualem scilicet se intentibus offert, manus quas potest et brachia spectans, palpat costas, humeros attrectat et lumbos: ut secum dum quod corporis sui membra, vel minus, vel satis exilia sentit, pallorem oris ac colorem discernat. Ad omnia denique sua strenuus, ad communia piger. Vigilat in lecto, dormit in choro: cumque aliis psalientibus ad vigilias totas nocte dormitabit, post vigilias aliis in claustro quiescentibus (151) solus in oratorio remanet: excreeat, et tussit, gemitus ac suspiriis aures legis sedentium de angulo implet. Cum autem ex his quae singulariter, sed inaniter agit, apud simpliciores eius opinio excreverit, uti profecto opus habet, quos coram se unde prodeant non discernunt; dum miserum beatificant, in errorem inducunt (Isa. iii, 12).
segments.en: It is shameful to him who boasts himself above the rest, if he does not do something more than the rest, by which he may appear beyond them. Therefore what the common rule of the monastery, or the examples of the seniors, urge is not enough for him. Yet he does not strive to be better, but to be seen. He longs not to live better, but to seem to live, so that he may say: I am not as the rest of men (Luke 18:11). He is active in all that is his own, lazy in what is common. He watches in bed, sleeps in choir; while others chant at the night vigils he dozes, and after vigils, when others rest in the cloister, he alone remains in the oratory: he clears his throat, coughs, and fills the ears of those sitting in the corner with groans and sighs.

title.la: De sexto gradu superbiae, qui est arrogantia
title.en: The sixth step of pride, which is arrogance

segments.la: Credit quod audit, laudat quod agit, et quod intendat non attendit. Obliviscitur intentionem dum amplectitur opinionem. Quique de omni alia re plus sibi credit, quam aliis, de se solo plus aliis credit, quam sibi: ut non iam verbis, oris, aut sola operum ostentatione suam praeferat religionem, sed intimo cordis credat affectu omnibus se sanctiorem, et quidquid de se laudatum agnoverit, non ignorantiae aut benevolentiæ laudatoris, sed suis meritis arroganter ascribit. Unde post singularitatem sextum sibi gradum iure arrogantia vindicat. Post hanc praesumptio invenitur, in qua septimus gradus constituitur.
segments.en: He believes what he hears, praises what he does, and does not attend to what he intends. He forgets intention while he embraces reputation. In every other matter he trusts himself more than others; in himself alone he trusts others more than himself—so that he no longer prefers his religion only by words of the mouth or by show of works, but in the inmost affection of the heart believes himself holier than all, and whatever praise he hears of himself he arrogantly ascribes not to the ignorance or kindness of the praiser, but to his own merits. Hence after singularity, arrogance justly claims the sixth step. After this, presumption is found, in which the seventh step is set.

title.la: De septimo gradu superbiae, qui est praesumptio
title.en: The seventh step of pride, which is presumption

segments.la: Qui enim alios se praecellere putat, quomodo plus de se, quam de aliis non praesumat? In conventibus residet, in consiliis primus respondet: non vocatus accedit, non iussus se intromittit: reordinat, ordinata, recrucit facta. Quidquid ipse non fecerit aut ordinaverit, nec recte factum, nec pulchre existimat ordinatum, factum iudicantes, praeiudicat iudicaturis. Si, cum tempus advenerit, non promoveatur ad Prioratum, suum abbatem aut invidum iudicat, aut deceptum. Quod si iunioribus ei aliqua obedientia iniuncta fuerit, indignatur, aspernatur, arbitrans se non esse ministerium occupandum, sed ad se magis seniori idoneum. Sed qui sic promptulus ad omnia se magis temere, quam libere consuevit ingerere, impossibile est eum aliquando non errare. Ad praelatum autem pertinet errantem arguere. Sed quomodo culpam etiam confitebitur, qui nec esse putat, nec agnari culpabilis patitur? Proinde cum ei displicet, crescit, non amputatur. Si ergo cum potutus fuerit, declinare cor eius defensionis in verba pellatur, in octavum gradum, qui dicitur defensio peccatorum, noveris corruisse.
segments.en: For he who thinks himself above others—how shall he not presume more of himself than of others? He sits in assemblies, answers first in councils; he comes uncalled, puts himself in unbidden. If, when the time comes, he is not promoted to the priorate, he judges his abbot either envious or deceived. If some obedience is enjoined on him with juniors, he is indignant, thinking the ministry not for him to occupy, but himself more fit for a senior’s place. But it is impossible that one so eager to thrust himself into everything should not sometime err. It belongs to the prelate to rebuke the one who errs. But how will he confess a fault who does not think it is one, and will not suffer himself to be known as blameable? If therefore, when he is rebuked, his heart turns aside into words of defense, know that he has fallen into the eighth step, which is called the defense of sins.

title.la: De octavo gradu superbiae, qui est defensio peccatorum
title.en: The eighth step of pride, which is defense of sins

segments.la: Multis vero modis fiunt excusationes in peccatis. Aut enim dicit qui se excusat: Non feci; aut, Feci quidem, sed male feci; aut, Si male, non tamen male; aut, Si tamen male, non mala intentione. Si autem et de illa, sicut Adam, vel Eva, convicitur, transferre nititur excusare se aliorum. Sed qui procaciter etiam aperta defendit, quando occultas et malas cogitationes, cordi suo advenientes, humiliter revelaret abbati?
segments.en: Excuses in sins are made in many ways. For either he who excuses himself says, I did not do it; or, I did it, but I did not do it badly; or, If badly, not very badly; or, If badly, not with a bad intention. And if he is convicted even of that, like Adam or Eve, he tries to shift the excuse onto others. But he who shamelessly defends even what is open—when would he humbly reveal to the abbot the hidden and evil thoughts that come to his heart?

title.la: De nono gradu superbiae, qui est simulata confessio
title.en: The ninth step of pride, which is feigned confession

segments.la: Licet vero genera haec excusationis eatenus mala iudicentur, quatenus ore prophetico verba malitiae appellentur (Psal. cxl, 4); multo tamen perniciosior est fallax ac superba confessio, quam procax et obstinata defensio. Nonnulli enim, cum de apertioribus arguuntur, scientes quod si se defenderent, sibi non crederetur, subtilius inveniunt argumentum defensionis, verba respondentes dolosae confessionis. Est quippe, ut scriptum est, qui nequiter humiliat se, et interiora eius plena sunt dolo (Eccli. xix, 23). Vultus demittitur, prosternitur corpus: aliquas sibi lacrymulas extorquent, si possunt; vocem suspiriis, verba gemitibus interrumpunt. Nec solum qui eiusmodi est, obiecta non excusat, sed ipse quoque culpam exaggerat: ut dum impossibile aliquid aut incredibile culpae suae ore ipsius additum audis, etiam illud, quod ratum putabas, discredere possis; et ex eo quod falsum esse non dubitas dum confitetur, in dubium veniat quod quasi certum tenebatur. Dumque affirmant quod credi nolunt, confitendo culpam defendunt, et aperiendo tegunt: quando et confessio laudabiliter sonat in ore, et adhuc iniquitas occultatur in corde: quatenus magis ex humilitate quam ex veritate confiteri putet qui audit, aptans eis illud Scripturae: Iustus in principio sermonis accusator est sui (Prov. xviii, 17). Malunt enim apud homines veritate periclitari, quam humilitate, cum apud Deum periclitentur utrinque. Aut si adeo culpa manifesta sit quod nulla penitus versutia tegi possit, nihilominus tamen vocem, non cor poenitentis assumunt, qua notam, non culpam deleant, dum ignorantiam manifestae transgressionis, decore recompensant publicae confessionis.
segments.en: Though these kinds of excuse are judged evil insofar as the prophet’s mouth calls them words of malice (Ps. 140:4), much more ruinous is a false and proud confession than a shameless and obstinate defense. For some, when charged with what is more open, knowing that if they defended themselves they would not be believed, find a subtler argument of defense, answering with the words of a deceitful confession. There is one, as it is written, who wickedly humbles himself, and his inward parts are full of deceit (Sir. 19:23). The face is cast down, the body prostrated: they wring out a few little tears, if they can; they interrupt the voice with sighs, the words with groans. Not only does a man of this sort not excuse what is charged, but he himself even exaggerates the fault: so that when you hear something impossible or incredible added to his guilt by his own mouth, you may be able to disbelieve even that which you thought established; and from the fact that you do not doubt that what he confesses is false, that which was held as almost certain may come into doubt. And while they affirm what they do not wish to be believed, by confessing they defend the fault, and by opening they cover it: when the confession sounds praiseworthy in the mouth, and wickedness is still hidden in the heart: so that he who hears may think they confess more from humility than from truth, applying to them that saying of Scripture: The just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech (Prov. 18:17). For they would rather be at risk among men in truthfulness than in humility, while before God they are at risk in both. Or if the fault is so manifest that it can be covered by no cunning at all, they nevertheless take the voice, not the heart, of a penitent, that they may wipe out the mark, not the guilt, while they make up for the ignoring of an open transgression with the credit of a public confession.

segments.la: Gloriosa res humilitas, qua ipsa quoque superbia palliare se appetit, ne vilescat! Sed haec cito tergiversatio a praelato deprehenditur, si ad hanc superbam humilitatem non leviter flectitur, quo magis dissimulet culpam, vel differat poenam. Vasa figuli probat fornax, et tribulatio vere poenitentes discernit. Qui enim veraciter poenitet, laborem poenitentiae non abhorret: sed quidquid sibi pro culpa quam odit iniungitur, tacita conscientia patienter amplectitur. In ipsa quoque obedientia duris ac contrariis rebus obortis, quibuslibet irrogatis iniuriis, sustinens non lassescit, ut in quarto gradu se stare indicet humilitatis. Cuius vero simulata confessio est, una vel levi contumelia, aut exigua poena interrogatus, iam humilitatem simulare, iam simulationem dissimulare non potest. Murmurat, frendet, irascitur; nec in quarto stare humilitatis, sed in nonum superbiae gradum corruisse probatur, qui secundum quod descriptus est, recte simulata confessio appellari potest. Quanta putas tunc confusio sit in corde superbi, cum fraus decipitur, pax amittitur, laus minuitur, nec culpa diluitur? Tandem notatur ab omnibus, iudicatur ab omnibus: eoque vehementius omnes indignantur, quo falsum conspiciunt quidquid de eo prius opinabantur. Tunc opus est praelato, ut eo minus illi parcendum putet, quo magis omnes offenderet, si uni parceret.
segments.en: A glorious thing is humility, in which pride itself seeks to cloak itself, lest it become cheap! But this evasion is soon detected by the superior, if he is not lightly bent by this proud humility to pass over the fault, or to postpone the penalty. The furnace tries the potter’s vessels, and tribulation distinguishes those who truly repent. For he who truly repents does not shrink from the labor of repentance: but whatever is enjoined on him for the fault he hates, he embraces with a silent conscience, patiently. In that very obedience, when hard and contrary things arise, when any injuries are inflicted, he does not grow weary in bearing them, so that he may show that he stands in the fourth degree of humility. But he whose confession is feigned, when faced with one slight insult or a small penalty, can no longer pretend humility, nor hide the pretence. He murmurs, gnashes, grows angry; and it is proved that he does not stand in the fourth step of humility, but has fallen to the ninth of pride, which, according to what has been described, may rightly be called feigned confession. How great, think you, is then the confusion in the proud man’s heart, when the fraud is detected, peace is lost, praise is lessened, and the fault is not washed away? At last he is marked by all, judged by all: and all are the more vehemently indignant, the more they see that whatever they had formerly thought of him was false. Then it is the superior’s part to think him the less to be spared, the more he would offend all if he spared one.

title.la: De decimo gradu superbiae, qui est rebellio
title.en: The tenth step of pride, which is rebellion

segments.la: Hic nisi eum miseratio superna respiciat, (quod valde difficile talibus est) universorum iudiciis tacitus acquiescat; frontosus mox et impudens factus, tanto deterius, quanto desperatius in decimum gradum per rebellionem corruit: quippe prius latenter arrogans fratres contempserat, iam patenter inobediens etiam magistrum contemnit.
segments.en: Unless heavenly mercy looks on this man, so that—which is very hard for such—he quietly accepts the judgments of all, he soon becomes shameless and defiant, and falls so much the worse, as more despairingly, to the tenth step by rebellion: for whereas before, secretly arrogant, he had despised the brethren, now openly disobedient he despises even the master.

segments.la: Sciendum autem est, quod omnes gradus, quos in duodecim partitus sum, in tres tantummodo colligi possunt: ut in sex superioribus contemptus fratrum, in quatuor sequentibus contemptus magistri, in duobus, qui restant, consummetur contemptus Dei. Notandum quoque, quod hi duo superbiae gradus ultimi, qui et humilitatis ascendendo primi inveniuntur; sicut extra congregationem ascendendi sunt, ita in congregatione descendi non possunt. Quod autem ante ascendi debeant, ex hoc aperte datur intelligi, quod de tertio gradu in Regula legitur: Tertius, inquit, gradus est, ut quis pro Dei amore omni obedientia se subdat maiori (Regul. vii, 31). Si ergo in tertio gradu subiectio collocatur, quae procul dubio fit, quando novitius primum conventui sociatur; consequens est, quod duo iam anteriores transcensi intelligantur. Denique ubi fratrum concordiam, et magistri sententiam monachus spernit, quid ultra in monasterio, nisi scandalum facit?
segments.en: It should be known that all the steps I have divided into twelve can be gathered into three only: so that in the six higher ones contempt of the brethren, in the four that follow contempt of the master, in the two that remain, contempt of God is completed. It should also be noted that these last two steps of pride, which in going up are found first in humility, as they are climbed outside the community, so they cannot be descended in the community. That they must be climbed beforehand is clearly given to be understood from this, that of the third degree it is read in the Rule: The third degree, it says, is that a man, for the love of God, submit himself with all obedience to a superior (Rule 7.31). If therefore subjection is placed in the third degree, which beyond doubt takes place when the novice is first joined to the community, it follows that the two earlier ones are understood to have been already passed. Finally, when a monk scorns the brethren’s concord and the master’s sentence, what does he do further in the monastery except make scandal?

title.la: De undecimo gradu superbiae, qui est libertas peccandi
title.en: The eleventh step of pride, which is freedom to sin

segments.la: Post decimum itaque gradum, qui rebellio dictus est, expulsus vel egressus de monasterio statim excipitur ab undecimo. Et tunc ingreditur vias, quae videntur hominibus bonae, quarum finis (nisi foris Deus eas illi seperit) demerget eum in profundum inferni, id est in contemptum Dei. Impius siquidem cum venerit in profundum malorum, contemnit (Prov. xviii, 3). Potest autem undecimus gradus appellari libertas peccandi, per quam monachus, cum iam nec magistrum videt quem timeat, nec fratres quos revereatur, tanto securius, quanto liberius sua desideria implere delectatur, a quibus in monasterio tam pudore, quam timore prohibebatur. Sed etsi iam vel fratres, vel abbatem non timet, nondum tamen Dei penitus formidine caret. Hac ratio, tenuter adhuc submurmurans, voluntati proponit, nec sine aliqua dubitatione quosque primum illicia perficit; sed, sicut in capite huius tractatus testat, pede tenim, non cursim vitiorum gurgitem intrat.
segments.en: So after the tenth step, which has been called rebellion, the man cast out or gone out of the monastery is at once received by the eleventh. Then he enters ways that seem good to men, whose end (unless God perhaps separates them from him) will plunge him into the depth of hell, that is into contempt of God. For when the wicked has come into the depth of evils, he despises (Prov. 18:3). The eleventh step may be called freedom to sin, by which the monk, when he no longer sees a master to fear or brethren to revere, delights to fulfill his desires all the more securely as more freely—desires from which in the monastery he was held back by shame as well as fear. Yet though he no longer fears brethren or abbot, he has not yet wholly lost the fear of God. For this reason, still faintly murmuring, reason sets itself against the will, and he does not accomplish those first enticements without some hesitation; but, as this treatise said at the start, he enters the gulf of vices step by step, not at a run.

title.la: De duodecimo gradu superbiae qui est consuetudo peccandi
title.en: The twelfth step of pride, which is the habit of sinning

segments.la: Postquam terribili Dei iudicio prima flagitia impunitas sequitur, experta voluptas libenter repetita libidini blanditur. Consuescentia revincitur ratio, ligat consuetudo. Trahitur in profundum malorum, traditur captivus filii vitiorum, ita ut carnalium voragine desiderium absorptus, suae rationis conscia timorata, dicat insipiens in corde suo: Non est Deus (Psal. xiii, 1). Iam indifferenter libeat pro liciis iam ab illicitis cogitandis, patrandis, investiendis: nullius, manes, vel potius non prohibentur: quidquid in cor, in buccam, in manum venerit, satur, garrit, et operatur, malevolus, vaniloquus, facinorosus. Quemadmodum denique ascensis omnibus gradibus, corde iam alacri et absque labore iustus ambulabit in via: somnis impius eisdem, pro malo suo non rene gubernans, non timoris freno retentans, inius festinat ad mortem. Medii sunt qui fatigantur, qui laborant. Nam tunc nisi cruciatur gehennae prius retardati consuetudine, descendendo oendendo laborant. Supremus tantum et infimus currunt absque impedimento, et absque labore. Istum hinc, ast illum ille festinat; alter alteriori perditioni. Istum almusitudo charitas, hunc proclivioris facit. In altero amor, in altero cupiditas non senit. In illo denique perfecta, in isto consummata iniquitas coram mittit. Illi veritas, huic caecitas dat securitatem. ergo duodecimus gradus appellari consuetudo solet, qua Dei metus amittitur, devotio extinguitur.
segments.en: After, by the terrible judgment of God, the first crimes go unpunished, pleasure once tasted is gladly repeated and flatters lust. Habit overcomes reason; custom binds. He is drawn into the depth of evils, handed over captive to the sons of vices, so that, swallowed in the gulf of fleshly desire, the fool says in his heart: There is no God (Ps. 13:1). As the just man, when all the steps have been climbed, will walk the way with a ready heart and without labor, so the wicked man, not governed for his own good, not held back by the bridle of fear, hurries to death. Only the highest and the lowest run without hindrance and without labor. The twelfth step is commonly called habit, by which the fear of God is lost and devotion is put out.

title.la: Quomodo orandum pro desperatis, et mortuis secundum animam
title.en: How we should pray for the desperate, and for those dead according to the soul

segments.la: Pro tali iam, inquit Ioannes apostolus, non dico ut quis oret (I Ioan. v, 16). Sed numquid dicis, o Apostole, ut quis desperet? Imo gemat qui illum amat. Non praesumat orare, nec desistat plorare. Quid est quod dico? An forte ullum remanet spei refugium, ubi oratio non invenit locum? Audi credentem, sperantem, nec tamen orantem. Domine, inquit, si fuisses hic, frater meus non fuisset mortuus. Magna fides, qua credidit sua praesentia Dominum mortem prohibere potuisse, si adfuisset. Modo autem quid? Absit ut quem credidit vivum posse servare, mortuum dubitet posse resuscitare. Sed et nunc, inquit, scio quia quaecumque poposceris, dabit tibi Deus. Deinde quaerenti ubi posuissent eum, respondet: Veni et vide. Quamobrem? O Martha, magna nobis tuae fidei insignia tribuis; sed quomodo cum tanta fide diffidis? Veni, inquis, et vide. Cur, si non desperas, non sequeris, et dicis: Et resuscita? Si autem desperas, cur magistrum sine causa fatigas? An forte fides aliquando recipit, quod oratio non praesumit? Denique appropinquantem cadaveri prohibes, et dicis: Domine, iam fetet; quatriduanus enim est (Ioan. xi, 21, 22, 34, 39). Desperando dicis hoc, an dissimulando? Sic quippe ipse Dominus post resurrectionem finxit se longius ire (Luc. xxiv, 28), cum mallet cum discipulis remanere. O sanctae mulieres Christi familiares, si fratrem vestrum amatis, cur eius misericordiam non flagitatis, de cuius potentia dubitare, de pietate diffidere non potestis? Respondent: Sic melius tamquam non orantes oramus, sic efficacius tamquam diffidentes confidimus. Exhibemus fidem, perhibemus affectum: scit ipse, cui non est opus ut aliquid dicatur, quid desideremus. Scimus quidem quod omnia potest: sed hoc tam grande miraculum, tam novum, tam inauditum, etsi eius subest potentiae, multum tamen excedit universa merita humilitatis nostrae. Sufficit nobis potentiae locum, pietati dare occasionem, malentes patienter exspectare quid velit, quam impudenter quaerere quod forsitan nolit. Denique quod nostris meritis deest, verecundia fortasse supplebit. Petri quoque post gravem lapsum lacrymas quidem video, sed precem non audio: nec tamen de indulgentia dubito.
segments.en: For such a one, says the Apostle John, I do not say that anyone should pray (1 John 5:16). But do you say, O Apostle, that anyone should despair? Rather let him groan who loves that man. Let him not presume to pray, and not cease to weep. What is this that I say? Is there perhaps some refuge of hope left, where prayer finds no place? Hear one who believes, who hopes, and yet does not pray. Lord, she says, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Great faith, by which she believed the Lord’s presence could have prevented death if he had been there. And now? Far be it that she who believed he could keep a living man should doubt he can raise a dead one. Yet now, she says, I know that whatever you ask, God will give you. Then, when he asks where they had laid him, she answers: Come and see. Why? O Martha, you give us great marks of your faith; but how, with such faith, do you distrust? Come, you say, and see. Why, if you do not despair, do you not go on and say: And raise him? But if you despair, why do you tire the Master without cause? Is it perhaps that faith sometimes receives what prayer does not presume to ask? Then, as he draws near the corpse, you hold him back and say: Lord, he already stinks; for he has been dead four days (John 11:21, 22, 34, 39). Do you say this in despair, or in pretence? So the Lord himself after the resurrection made as though he would go farther (Luke 24:28), when he would rather remain with the disciples. O holy women, friends of Christ, if you love your brother, why do you not beg his mercy, of whose power you cannot doubt, of whose pity you cannot distrust? They answer: So we pray better as if not praying, so we trust more effectually as if distrusting. We show faith, we hold back affection: he himself knows, who has no need that anything be said, what we desire. We know indeed that he can do all things: but this miracle, so great, so new, so unheard of, though it lies within his power, still far exceeds all the merits of our humility. It is enough for us to have given place to his power, occasion to his pity, preferring to wait patiently for what he wills rather than shamelessly to ask what he may not will. And what our merits lack, modesty will perhaps supply. In Peter too after his heavy fall I see tears, but I do not hear a prayer: yet I do not doubt of pardon.

segments.la: Disce et in Matre Domini magnam in mirabilibus fidem habere, in magna fide verecundiam retinere. Disce verecundia decorare fidem, reprimere praesumptionem. Vinum, inquit, non habent (Ioan. ii, 3). Quam breviter, quam reverenter suggessit, unde pie fuit sollicita! Et ut discas in huiusmodi magis pie gemere, quam petere praesumptuose, pietatis aestum pudoris temperans umbra, conceptam precis fiduciam verecunde suppressit. Non frontose accessit, non palam locuta est, ut audacter coram omnibus diceret: Obsecro, fili, deficit vinum, contristantur convivae, confunditur sponsus; ostende quid possis. Sed licet haec aut multo plura pectus aestuans, fervens loqueretur affectus, privatim tamen potentem pia Filium mater adit, non potentiam tentans, sed voluntatem explorans. Vinum, inquit, non habent. Quid modestius? Quid fidelius? Non defuit pietati fides, voci gravitas, efficacia voto. Si ergo illa, cum mater sit, sese matrem oblita non audet petere miraculum vini, ego vile mancipium, cui permagnum est Filii simul ac Matris esse vernaculum, qua fronte praesumo pro vita petere quatriduani?
