segments.en: Learn also in the Mother of the Lord to have great faith in marvels, and in great faith to keep modesty. Learn to adorn faith with modesty, and to check presumption. They have no wine, she says (John 2:3). How briefly, how reverently she suggested what she was piously anxious about! And that you may learn in such things to groan more piously than to ask presumptuously, tempering the heat of her piety with a shade of shame, she modestly suppressed the confidence of the prayer she had conceived. She did not come forward boldly, she did not speak openly, so as to say audaciously before all: I beg you, son, the wine has failed, the guests are saddened, the bridegroom is put to confusion; show what you can do. But although her burning heart, her fervent affection, might have spoken these things or many more, yet the devout Mother privately approached her powerful Son, not testing his power but exploring his will. They have no wine, she says. What more modest? What more faithful? Faith was not wanting to her piety, gravity to her voice, efficacy to her wish. If therefore she, though she is his Mother, forgetting herself as mother, does not dare to ask the miracle of wine, I, a cheap slave, to whom it is a great thing to be a household servant of Son and Mother at once—with what face do I presume to ask life for one four days dead?

segments.la: Duo etiam in Evangelio caeci visum, alter accepisse, alter recepisse leguntur: alter quem amiserat, alter quem nunquam habuerat; unus scilicet excaecatus, alter caecus natus. Sed qui excaecatus, miserabilibus mirisque clamoribus miram misericordiam meruit; qui vero caecus natus, tanto misericordius, quanto mirabilius nullis suis precibus praeventum, sui illuminatoris beneficium nihilominus sensit. Illi denique dictum est, Fides tua te salvum fecit: huic autem non (Luc. xviii, 35–43; Ioan. ix). Duos quoque recenter mortuos, tertium iam quatriduanum, lego resuscitatos: solam tamen Archisynagogi filiam, in domo adhuc positam, precibus patris; duos autem ex insperata magnitudine pietatis (Marc. v, 35–43; Luc. vii, 11–15; Ioan. xi).
segments.en: Two blind men also in the Gospel are read to have received or recovered sight: one the sight he had lost, the other that he had never had; one, that is, who had been blinded, the other born blind. But the one who had been blinded earned marvellous mercy by piteous and wondrous cries; the one born blind, the more mercifully as more marvellously, felt the benefit of his enlightener, not preceded by any prayers of his own. To the former it was said, Your faith has made you whole; to the latter, not (Luke 18:35–43; John 9). I also read of two recently dead, and a third already four days dead, raised: only the synagogue-ruler’s daughter, still in the house, by her father’s prayers; the other two by an unexpected greatness of pity (Mark 5:35–43; Luke 7:11–15; John 11).

segments.la: Simili etiam forma si contigerit (quod Deus avertat) aliquem de fratribus nostris, non in corpore, sed in anima mori, quamdiu adhuc inter nos erit, pulsabo et ego meis qualiscumque peccator, pulsabo et fratrum precibus Salvatorem. Si revixerit, lucrati erimus fratrem: sin vero non mereamur exaudiri, ubi iam vel tolerare vivos, vel tolerari a vivis non poterit, sed incipiet efferri, semper quidem fideliter gemo, sed iam non ita fiducialiter oro. Non aperte audeo dicere: Veni, Domine, suscita mortuum nostrum: corde tamen suspenso, tremulus intus clamare non cesso: Si forte, si forte, si forte, desiderium pauperum exaudiet Dominus, praeparationem cordis eorum audiet auris eius (Psal. x, 17); et illud: Numquid mortuis facies mirabilia, aut medici suscitabunt, et confitebuntur tibi? Et de quatriduano: Numquid narrabit aliquis in sepulcro misericordiam tuam, aut veritatem tuam in perditione? (Psal. lxxxvii, 11–12.) Potest interim Salvator, si vult, insperate et improvise occurrere nobis, lacrymisque portantium motus, non precibus, mortuo vitam reddere vivis, aut certe iam sepultum revocare a mortuis. Mortuum autem dixerim illum, qui sua peccata defendens, in octavum iam corruit gradum. A mortuo enim, tamquam qui non est, perit confessio (Eccli. xvii, 26). Post decimum vero, qui tertius est ab octavo, iam effertur in libertatem peccandi, quando expellitur a consortio monasterii. At postquam quartum transierit, iam recte quatriduanus dicitur, dum in quintum decidens per consuetudinem sepelitur.
segments.en: If in like form it should happen (which God forbid) that any of our brethren die not in the body but in the soul, as long as he is still among us I, sinner that I am, will knock, I will knock at the Saviour with my prayers and the brethren’s. If he lives again, we shall have gained our brother: but if we do not deserve to be heard, and he can no longer bear the living or be borne by them, and begins to be carried out, I still groan faithfully, but I no longer pray with the same confidence. I do not dare to say openly: Come, Lord, raise our dead: yet with a suspended heart, trembling within, I do not cease to cry: If perhaps, if perhaps, if perhaps the Lord will hear the desire of the poor, his ear will hear the preparation of their heart (Ps. 10:17); and that: Will you do wonders for the dead, or shall physicians raise them, and they confess to you? And of the four-days-dead: Shall anyone in the sepulchre declare your mercy, or your truth in destruction? (Ps. 87:11–12.) Meanwhile the Saviour, if he wills, can meet us unforeseen and unexpected, and, moved by the tears of the bearers, not by prayers, restore the dead man’s life to the living, or even recall from the dead one already buried. I would call dead the man who, defending his sins, has already fallen to the eighth step. For from the dead, as from one who is not, confession perishes (Sir. 17:26). After the tenth, which is third from the eighth, he is already carried out into freedom to sin, when he is expelled from the monastery’s company. And after he has passed the fourth, he is already rightly called four days dead, while falling into the fifth he is buried by habit.

segments.la: Absit autem a nobis, ut etiam pro talibus, etsi palam non praesumimus, vel in cordibus nostris orare cessemus: cum Paulus eos quoque lugeret, quos sine paenitentia mortuos sciret (II Cor. xii, 21). Etsi enim a communibus orationibus ipsi se excludunt, ab affectibus omnino non possunt. Viderint tamen, in quanto periculo sint pro quibus Ecclesia palam orare non audeat, quae fidenter etiam pro Iudaeis, pro haereticis, pro gentilibus orat. Cum enim in Parasceve nominatim oretur pro quibuslibet malis, nulla tamen mentio fit de excommunicatis.
segments.en: But God forbid that we should cease to pray in our hearts even for such, though we do not presume to do so openly: since Paul also mourned those whom he knew to have died without repentance (2 Cor. 12:21). For though they shut themselves out from the common prayers, they cannot at all from the affections. Let them see, however, in how great a danger they are for whom the Church does not dare to pray openly, who yet prays confidently even for Jews, for heretics, for the nations. For when on Good Friday prayer is made by name for any of the wicked, still no mention is made of the excommunicated.

segments.la: Dicis forsitan, frater Godefride, me aliud quam tu quaesisti, quam ipse promisi, tandem exhibuisse, cum pro gradibus humilitatis, superbiae gradus videar descripsisse. Ad quod ego: Non potui docere nisi quod didici. Non putavi congruum me describere ascensiones, qui plus descendere quam ascendere novi. Proponat tibi beatus Benedictus gradus humilitatis, quos ipse prius in corde suo disposuit: ego quid proponam non habeo, nisi ordinem meae descensionis, in quo tamen si diligenter inspicitur, via forsitan ascensionis reperitur. Si enim tibi Romam tendenti homo inde veniens obviaret, quaesitus viam, quid melius quam illam qua venit ostenderet? Dum castella, villas, urbes, fluvios ac montes, per quos transierit, nominat, suum denuntians iter, tuum tibi praenuntiat: ita ut eadem loca recognoscas eundo, quae ille pertransiit veniendo. In hac similiter nostra descensione gradus ascensorios fortasse reperies, quos ascendendo melius tu in tuo corde, quam in nostro codice legas.
segments.en: You may perhaps say, brother Godfrey, that I have at last shown something other than you asked and I promised, as if I seemed to describe the steps of pride rather than of humility. To which I say: I could not teach except what I have learned. I did not think it fitting that I should describe goings-up, who know more how to go down than to go up. Let blessed Benedict set before you the steps of humility, which he first arranged in his own heart: I have nothing to set before you except the order of my own descent, in which nevertheless, if it is carefully looked at, the way of ascent may perhaps be found. For if, as you are going toward Rome, a man coming thence should meet you, and you asked the way, what better could he show than the way by which he came? While he names the castles, villages, cities, rivers, and mountains through which he has passed, telling his own journey, he foretells yours: so that as you go you recognize the same places he passed as he came. In this downward course of ours you may likewise discover the upward steps, which you will better read by climbing them in your own heart than in our book.
